boundaries.evidence: J = empty is admitted: W_J = {1}, ^JW = S_n, and the two characters coincide on H_J = A, so M^J = N^J = H_v(n) with basis {H_w}. The definition is stated for arbitrary J including the empty and full index sets.

No vanishing case enters the definition: the scalars phi_+(H_s) = v^{-1} and phi_-(H_s) = -v are units of A = Z[v^{+-1}] satisfying the quadratic relation x^2 - (v^{-1}-v)x - 1 = 0, and no module is asserted to be zero.

The unit values phi_+(H_s) = v^{-1} and phi_-(H_s) = -v are displayed, and the identity w = 1 lies in ^JW and W^J; the quadratic relation of the normalized Hecke algebra is exactly what makes these the two characters. See the Definition.

The extremes J = empty (W_J = {1}) and J = S (^JW = {1}, modules free of rank one over A) lie inside the stated range J subseteq S and are recorded in the remarks; A is a Laurent ring, so no zero-divisor or singular-parameter degeneracy arises. See the Definition.

boundaries.reason: The definition involves no intervals or limiting processes; the only extremal data are the index extremes J = empty and J = S noted above.
Choice-free: the definition forms scalars and balanced tensor products over A; nothing is selected from a family of nonempty sets.
The Definition asserts no separate biconditional. Its character maps are restrictions of scalar homomorphisms on the full presented Hecke algebra; no subalgebra presentation is assumed.
There is no converse direction to check: the factorization w = ly is quoted from the supplier, and no iff is claimed in this item.

risk_review.notes: The scalar assignments satisfy every relation of the full normalized presentation and restrict to H_J. Balanced tensors have the specified right action; length-additive parabolic factorization supplies the indexing. J=empty, J=S and n=1 are admitted. Both signs and all module interfaces are preserved.

boundaries.evidence: J = empty is the regular case: W_J = {1}, W^J = W, and the block conventions reduce to the regular integral block, as recorded in (5). The stabilizer and label families are never empty since e is always available. See the Definition.

The vanishing simple coroot pairings define J = {i : <mu+rho, alpha_i^vee> = 0}. The zero pattern of the multiplicity matrix, (P(w.mu):Delta(w.mu)) = 1 and nonzero only above the head, is quoted from BGG reciprocity and the projective-standard label corollary. See the Definition.
The diagonal multiplicity (P(w.mu):Delta(w.mu)) = 1 and the identity element w = e of W^J are part of (4); the stabilizer proof for (2) starts from W_J containing the identity. See the Definition.

The singular case J != empty is the subject itself, and the most singular case J = S (mu = -rho) is included; (5) records that J = empty recovers the regular block, so no case is silently excluded. See the Definition.
Dot-antidominant mu is an endpoint of its dot orbit (mu + rho is antidominant), and W^J consists of the length-minimal elements of the cosets wW_J; both endpoint choices are part of the definition.
The Axiom of Choice is declared and inherited from the published block theory (enough projectives, Verma flags of projectives, Grothendieck bases); this definition adds no new selection.
w' . mu = w . mu implies w^{-1}w' in W_J: this is the forward half of the coset criterion derived from the stabilizer computation of (2). See the Definition.
w^{-1}w' in W_J implies w' . mu = w . mu: immediate from W_J subseteq the dot stabilizer, also proved in (2). See the Definition.

Let $(S,m)$ be a finite Coxeter matrix with presented group $W$, length $\ell$ and geometric representation $\sigma:W\to\mathrm{GL}_K(E)$ as in [[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]], [[def-hh-geometric-coxeter-representation-and-roots]] and [[lem-hh-dihedral-root-recurrence-and-root-sign]], and let $J\subseteq S$.

1. **Support and reduction.** For every $w\in W$ the set $S(w)$ of letters occurring in a reduced expression of $w$ is independent of the reduced expression, and every word in $S$ representing $w$ can be transformed into a reduced expression by repeatedly deleting two letters (Tits reduction, using only letters already present). Consequently
$$W_J=\langle J\rangle=\{w\in W:S(w)\subseteq J\}.$$
2. **Intrinsic parabolic presentation.** Let $W_J^\ast$ be the group presented by the restricted Coxeter matrix $(J,m|_J)$ in the sense of [[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]]. The canonical homomorphism $W_J^\ast\to W_J$, $s\mapsto s$, is an isomorphism. Hence $(W_J,J)$ is a Coxeter system, its intrinsic length function $\ell_J$ agrees with the ambient length $\ell$ on $W_J$, and $W_J\cap S=J$.
3. **Minimal coset representatives.** Every right coset $W_J a:=\{ua:u\in W_J\}$ ($a\in W$, [[def-coset]]) has a unique element $d$ of minimal length; it is characterized by $\ell(sd)>\ell(d)$ for all $s\in J$, and it satisfies
$$\ell(ud)=\ell(u)+\ell(d)\qquad\text{for all }u\in W_J .$$
Equivalently, every $w\in W$ has a unique factorization $w=u\,d$ with $u\in W_J$ and $d$ the minimal representative of the right coset $W_J d$, and then $\ell(w)=\ell(u)+\ell(d)$. By inversion ($w\mapsto w^{-1}$ preserves lengths and interchanges the two coset families $\{W_Ja\}$ and $\{aW_J\}$), every left coset $aW_J:=\{au:u\in W_J\}$ has a unique minimal element $d$, characterized by $\ell(ds)>\ell(d)$ for all $s\in J$ and satisfying $\ell(du)=\ell(d)+\ell(u)$ for all $u\in W_J$.
4. **Type A.** Let $n\ge2$, $S=\{s_1,\dots,s_{n-1}\}$ and $m(s_i,s_j):=3$ if $|i-j|=1$, $m(s_i,s_j):=2$ if $|i-j|>1$ (a Coxeter matrix of type $A_{n-1}$). Then $s_i\mapsto(i\ i+1)$ extends to an isomorphism $W\to S_n$ (the letters $1,\dots,n$ carry the library's symmetric group by the order-preserving identification with $\{0,\dots,n-1\}$, under which $(i\ i+1)$ is the adjacent transposition $(i-1\ i)$), and for every $w\in W$,
$$\ell(w)=\operatorname{inv}\bigl(\varphi(w)\bigr),$$
the inversion number of the corresponding permutation ([[def-inversions-inversion-number-and-sign]]). In particular a word in the $s_i$ is reduced if and only if its length equals the inversion number of its value.

Let $(S,m)$, $W$, $\ell$ and $I,J\subseteq S$ be as in
[[def-cg-parabolic-quotient-and-two-sided-minima]], so that $W_I$, $W^I$,
${}^IW$ and the descents $D_L,D_R$ have the meaning fixed there. Let
$V=\mathbb R^S$ with its Coxeter form $B$ and positive cone
$V_+=\{\sum_{s\in S}\lambda_se_s:\lambda_s\ge0\}$
([[def-cg-real-coxeter-form-and-reflection]]), let
$\rho:W\to\mathrm{GL}(V)$ be the canonical reflection homomorphism with root
system $\Phi=\Phi_+\sqcup\Phi_-$
([[def-cg-canonical-reflection-homomorphism]],
[[thm-cg-root-sign-and-simple-reflection-positivity]] (2)), and for
$I\subseteq S$ put

$$V_I:=\operatorname{span}\{e_s:s\in I\},\qquad \Phi_I:=\{\rho(w)e_s:w\in W_I,\ s\in I\}$$

([[def-linear-combination-and-span]]); here $V_\emptyset=\{0\}$ and
$\Phi_\emptyset=\emptyset$.

**(1) Intersections.** For all $I,J\subseteq S$,

$$W_I\cap W_J=W_{I\cap J}.$$

**(2) Parabolic root subsystems.** For every $I\subseteq S$ one has
$\rho(w)V_I=V_I$ for all $w\in W_I$; consequently

$$\Phi_I=\Phi\cap V_I=\{\alpha\in\Phi:\alpha\text{ is a real linear combination of the simple roots }e_s,\ s\in I\}.$$

Moreover $\Phi_I=\Phi_I^+\sqcup\Phi_I^-$ with
$\Phi_I^\pm:=\Phi_I\cap\Phi^\pm=\Phi^\pm\cap V_I$, and the reflections lying in
$W_I$ are exactly the elements $t_\alpha\in T$ with $\alpha\in\Phi_I^+$ in the
root-reflection dictionary of
[[thm-cg-root-inversion-formulas-and-strong-exchange]] (1).

**(3) Coset minima are global minima.** Let $I\subseteq S$, $w\in W$, and let
$d\in W^I$ be the unique element of $W^I\cap wW_I$, i.e. the unique $d\in W^I$
with $w\in dW_I$
([[def-cg-parabolic-quotient-and-two-sided-minima]] (2)). Then

$$\ell(d)\le\ell(x)\quad\text{for every }x\in wW_I,\qquad\text{and}\qquad \ell(d)=\ell(x)\iff x=d;$$

equivalently

$$W^I=\{d\in W:\ell(d)\le\ell(dv)\text{ for all }v\in W_I\},\qquad {}^IW=\{d\in W:\ell(d)\le\ell(vd)\text{ for all }v\in W_I\}.$$

Thus each set $wW_I$ contains exactly one element of $W^I$, namely its unique
element of minimum length, and symmetrically each right coset $W_Iw$ contains
exactly one element of ${}^IW$, namely its unique element of minimum length.

Let $(S,m)$ be a finite Coxeter matrix, let $W$ be the presented group with
length function $\ell$ ([[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]]), and
let $T=\{wsw^{-1}:w\in W,\ s\in S\}$ be the set of reflections of $W$
([[def-cg-canonical-reflection-homomorphism]]). Throughout, $I$ and $J$ denote
subsets of $S$.

**(1) Standard parabolic subgroups.** For $I\subseteq S$ put

$$W_I:=\langle s:s\in I\rangle\le W,$$

the subgroup generated by $I$ ([[def-generated-subgroup]]); $W_I$ is the
**standard parabolic subgroup** of $(W,S)$ of type $I$. Thus
$W_\emptyset=\{1\}$ and $W_S=W$. By
[[thm-hh-parabolic-minimal-representatives-and-length-additivity]] (1),(2): for
every $w\in W$ one has $w\in W_I$ if and only if $S(w)\subseteq I$, where
$S(w)$ is the (well-defined) set of letters of any reduced expression of $w$;
$(W_I,I)$ is a Coxeter system; its intrinsic length function agrees with
$\ell|_{W_I}$; and $W_I\cap S=I$.

**(2) Descents and the one-sided quotients.** For $w\in W$ put

$$D_L(w):=\{s\in S:\ell(sw)<\ell(w)\},\qquad D_R(w):=\{s\in S:\ell(ws)<\ell(w)\};$$

each of $\ell(sw)-\ell(w)$ and $\ell(ws)-\ell(w)$ lies in $\{\pm1\}$
([[thm-hh-coxeter-exchange-deletion-and-faithfulness]] (1)). Define

$$W^I:=\{w\in W:\ell(ws)>\ell(w)\text{ for all }s\in I\}=\{w\in W:D_R(w)\cap I=\emptyset\},$$

$${}^IW:=\{w\in W:\ell(sw)>\ell(w)\text{ for all }s\in I\}=\{w\in W:D_L(w)\cap I=\emptyset\}.$$

Conventions are fixed here: in ${}^IW$ the subset $I$ is tested on the left, in
$W^I$ it is tested on the right; $\ell(sw)$ means left multiplication by $s$
and $\ell(ws)$ right multiplication. The interpretation of these sets as sets
of coset representatives is not part of the definition; it is quoted from
[[thm-hh-parabolic-minimal-representatives-and-length-additivity]] (3) and
re-examined in [[thm-cg-parabolic-intersections-and-coset-factorization]] (3):
every $w\in W$ has a unique factorization

$$w=u\,d\qquad(u\in W_I,\ d\in{}^IW),\qquad \ell(w)=\ell(u)+\ell(d),$$

where $d$ is the unique element of minimal length in the right coset $W_Iw$, and
it satisfies $\ell(ud)=\ell(u)+\ell(d)$ for all $u\in W_I$; symmetrically every
$w\in W$ has a unique factorization

$$w=d\,v\qquad(d\in W^I,\ v\in W_I),\qquad \ell(w)=\ell(d)+\ell(v),$$

where $d$ is the unique element of minimal length in the left coset $wW_I$, and
it satisfies $\ell(dv)=\ell(d)+\ell(v)$ for all $v\in W_I$. Thus ${}^IW$
consists exactly of the elements of minimal length in the right cosets
$W_Iw=\{uw:u\in W_I\}$ and $W^I$ consists exactly of the elements of minimal
length in the sets $wW_I=\{wv:v\in W_I\}$. Inversion gives
$W^I=({}^IW)^{-1}$, because $\ell(x)=\ell(x^{-1})$ and $(sw)^{-1}=w^{-1}s$.

**(3) The two-sided quotients.** Define

$${}^IW^J:={}^IW\cap W^J=\{w\in W:\ell(sw)>\ell(w)\text{ for all }s\in I\ \text{ and }\ \ell(ws)>\ell(w)\text{ for all }s\in J\};$$

thus ${}^\emptyset W^J=W^J$, ${}^IW^\emptyset={}^IW$ and ${}^\emptyset
W^\emptyset=W$, and the members of ${}^IW^J$ are exactly the elements of $W$
with no left descent in $I$ and no right descent in $J$. Whether ${}^IW^J$ is a
set of representatives of the double cosets $W_IwW_J$ is again a theorem, not a
definition; it is proved in
[[thm-cg-double-coset-unique-minimum-and-normal-form]].

**(4) Parabolic subgroups and reflection subgroups.** A subgroup $H\le W$ is a
**parabolic subgroup** of $(W,S)$ if

$$H=wW_Iw^{-1}\qquad\text{for some }w\in W,\ I\subseteq S;$$

a parabolic subgroup with $w=1$ is *standard*. A subgroup $H\le W$ is a
**reflection subgroup** if $H=\langle H\cap T\rangle$, i.e. if $H$ is generated
by the reflections it contains. Every parabolic subgroup is a reflection
subgroup, since $wW_Iw^{-1}=\langle wsw^{-1}:s\in I\rangle$ and
$wsw^{-1}\in T$ for all $s\in S$, $w\in W$. No converse is asserted: it is not
claimed here that a subgroup generated by reflections is parabolic, and the
companion examples page computes test cases for the two distinctions created by
this definition --- standard parabolic versus parabolic, and reflection subgroup
versus parabolic subgroup.

Let $n\ge1$ and $A:=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$. For $n\ge2$, define the **normalized type-A Hecke algebra** $H_v(n)$ to be the associative unital $A$-algebra presented by generators $H_{s_1},\ldots,H_{s_{n-1}}$ with relations
$$H_{s_i}^2=1+(v^{-1}-v)H_{s_i},\qquad H_{s_i}H_{s_{i+1}}H_{s_i}=H_{s_{i+1}}H_{s_i}H_{s_{i+1}},\qquad H_{s_i}H_{s_j}=H_{s_j}H_{s_i}\quad(|i-j|>1).$$
For $n=1$, set $H_v(1):=A$.

Here $S_n=\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\ldots,n\})$, $s_i=(i\ i+1)$, and $\ell$ is inversion length as in [[def-symmetric-group]] and [[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]. For $w\in S_n$, let $T_w$ be the standard basis element of the generic Hecke algebra of [[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]], formed from any reduced expression of $w$, and after the coefficient specialization $q\mapsto v^{-2}$ put $H_w:=v^{\ell(w)}T_w$. Equivalently, $H_w=H_{s_{i_1}}\cdots H_{s_{i_k}}$ for a reduced expression $w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_k}$. The standard-basis theorem [[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]] and rescaling by units show that $\{H_w:w\in S_n\}$ is an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$.

Right multiplication by a generator is
$$H_wH_{s_i}=H_{ws_i}\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)+1,\qquad H_wH_{s_i}=H_{ws_i}+(v^{-1}-v)H_w\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)-1.$$

**Dictionary with the generic normalization.** If the generic parameter in [[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]] is denoted by $q$, its relation is $T_i^2=(q-1)T_i+q$. The coefficient map $q\mapsto v^{-2}$ is the stated specialization, and $H_{s_i}=vT_i$. This gives $H_{s_i}^2=1+(v^{-1}-v)H_{s_i}$; the braid and commutation relations are unchanged. The two multiplication cases above are the standard-basis rule after the same rescaling.

**Bar assignment.** Let $F$ be the free associative $\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$-algebra on the generator symbols. Define the semilinear algebra map $\iota_0:F\to F$ by $\iota_0(v)=v^{-1}$ and $\iota_0(H_{s_i})=H_{s_i}-(v^{-1}-v)$. In the quotient $H_v(n)$, the quadratic relation makes this latter element the two-sided inverse $H_{s_i}^{-1}$. The next lemma proves that $\iota_0$ preserves the defining ideal and descends to a well-defined involution $\iota$ on $H_v(n)$.

All items on this page use this normalization. It agrees with Elias–Williamson §3.2 under $H_x=v^{\ell(x)}T_x$ and $q=v^{-2}$.

In the generic type-A Hecke algebra $H_v(n)$ over $A=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ with
generators $T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$, the quadratic relations
$(T_i-v)(T_i+1)=0$, the braid relations and the distant commutations, and with
$T_w$ the product of the $T_i$ along a reduced word for $w\in S_n$
([[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]):

1. $\{T_w:w\in S_n\}$ is an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$; in particular $H_v(n)$ is
free of rank $n!$ over $A$;
2. for every $w\in S_n$ and every $1\le i\le n-1$,
$$T_wT_i=T_{ws_i}\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)+1,\qquad T_wT_i=(v-1)T_w+v\,T_{ws_i}\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)-1,$$
where $\ell$ is the inversion length of $S_n$
([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]); consequently the rule rewrites
every monomial in the generators as an $A$-linear combination of the $T_w$.

No choice principle is used.

In $H_v(n)$ there is a unique $A$-semilinear unital ring involution, denoted by a bar, with $\bar v=v^{-1}$ and $\overline{H_{s_i}}=H_{s_i}^{-1}$. It is multiplicative and satisfies $\overline{\overline{H_w}}=H_w$ and $\overline{H_w}=H_{w^{-1}}^{-1}$ for every $w\in S_n$; consequently each $H_w$ is invertible and $\overline{H_{w^{-1}}}=H_w^{-1}$.

Let $\le$ be the rank-inequality order on the zero-based $S_n$ of [[def-bruhat-order-on-the-symmetric-group]], and identify it with the one-based realization by shifting inputs and values by $1$. (a) This order is the strong Bruhat order of type A: the transitive closure of covers $x\to tx$ where $t$ is a transposition and $\ell(tx)=\ell(x)+1$. (b) If $y\le w$ then $\ell(y)\le\ell(w)$, with equality iff $y=w$; every saturated chain has $\ell(w)-\ell(y)$ steps; and $y\le w$ iff $y^{-1}\le w^{-1}$. (c) $y\le w$ iff for every reduced expression $w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_k}$, $y$ is a reduced subword. (d) For every simple reflection $s$, if $y\le w$ and $\ell(sy)>\ell(y)$, then $y\le sw$; if $y\le w$ and $\ell(sw)<\ell(w)$, then $sy\le w$. (e) Every interval $[y,w]$ is finite; if $y\le w$, then $[y,w]=\{y\}\cup\bigcup_{y\to a\le w}[a,w]$.

By inversion ($w\mapsto w^{-1}$ preserves lengths and interchanges the two coset families $\{W_Ja\}$ and $\{aW_J\}$), every left coset $aW_J:=\{au:u\in W_J\}$ has a unique minimal element $d$, characterized by $\ell(ds)>\ell(d)$ for all $s\in J$ and satisfying $\ell(du)=\ell(d)+\ell(u)$ for all $u\in W_J$.
4. **Type A.** Let $n\ge2$, $S=\{s_1,\dots,s_{n-1}\}$ and $m(s_i,s_j):=3$ if $|i-j|=1$, $m(s_i,s_j):=2$ if $|i-j|>1$ (a Coxeter matrix of type $A_{n-1}$). Then $s_i\mapsto(i\ i+1)$ extends to an isomorphism $W\to S_n$ (the letters $1,\dots,n$ carry the library's symmetric group by the order-preserving identification with $\{0,\dots,n-1\}$, under which $(i\ i+1)$ is the adjacent transposition $(i-1\ i)$), and for every $w\in W$,
$$\ell(w)=\operatorname{inv}\bigl(\varphi(w)\bigr),$$
the inversion number of the corresponding permutation ([[def-inversions-inversion-number-and-sign]]). In particular a word in the $s_i$ is reduced if and only if its length equals the inversion number of its value.

Let $(S,m)$ be a finite Coxeter matrix with presented group $W$, length $\ell$ and geometric representation $\sigma:W\to\mathrm{GL}_K(E)$ as in [[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]], [[def-hh-geometric-coxeter-representation-and-roots]] and [[lem-hh-dihedral-root-recurrence-and-root-sign]], and let $J\subseteq S$.

1. **Support and reduction.** For every $w\in W$ the set $S(w)$ of letters occurring in a reduced expression of $w$ is independent of the reduced expression, and every word in $S$ representing $w$ can be transformed into a reduced expression by repeatedly deleting two letters (Tits reduction, using only letters already present). Consequently
$$W_J=\langle J\rangle=\{w\in W:S(w)\subseteq J\}.$$
2. **Intrinsic parabolic presentation.** Let $W_J^\ast$ be the group presented by the restricted Coxeter matrix $(J,m|_J)$ in the sense of [[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]]. The canonical homomorphism $W_J^\ast\to W_J$, $s\mapsto s$, is an isomorphism. Hence $(W_J,J)$ is a Coxeter system, its intrinsic length function $\ell_J$ agrees with the ambient length $\ell$ on $W_J$, and $W_J\cap S=J$.
3. **Minimal coset representatives.** Every right coset $W_J a:=\{ua:u\in W_J\}$ ($a\in W$, [[def-coset]]) has a unique element $d$ of minimal length; it is characterized by $\ell(sd)>\ell(d)$ for all $s\in J$, and it satisfies
$$\ell(ud)=\ell(u)+\ell(d)\qquad\text{for all }u\in W_J .$$
Equivalently, every $w\in W$ has a unique factorization $w=u\,d$ with $u\in W_J$ and $d$ the minimal representative of the right coset $W_J d$, and then $\ell(w)=\ell(u)+\ell(d)$. By inversion ($w\mapsto w^{-1}$ preserves lengths and interchanges the two coset families $\{W_Ja\}$ and $\{aW_J\}$), every left coset $aW_J:=\{au:u\in W_J\}$ has a unique minimal element $d$, characterized by $\ell(ds)>\ell(d)$ for all $s\in J$ and satisfying $\ell(du)=\ell(d)+\ell(u)$ for all $u\in W_J$.
4. **Type A.** Let $n\ge2$, $S=\{s_1,\dots,s_{n-1}\}$ and $m(s_i,s_j):=3$ if $|i-j|=1$, $m(s_i,s_j):=2$ if $|i-j|>1$ (a Coxeter matrix of type $A_{n-1}$). Then $s_i\mapsto(i\ i+1)$ extends to an isomorphism $W\to S_n$ (the letters $1,\dots,n$ carry the library's symmetric group by the order-preserving identification with $\{0,\dots,n-1\}$, under which $(i\ i+1)$ is the adjacent transposition $(i-1\ i)$), and for every $w\in W$,
$$\ell(w)=\operatorname{inv}\bigl(\varphi(w)\bigr),$$
the inversion number of the corresponding permutation ([[def-inversions-inversion-number-and-sign]]). In particular a word in the $s_i$ is reduced if and only if its length equals the inversion number of its value.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$ and $\sigma\in S_n=\operatorname{Sym}(n)$. An
**inversion** of $\sigma$ is a pair $(i,j)$ with $i<j<n$ and
$\sigma(i)>\sigma(j)$. The **inversion set** and **inversion number** are

$$\operatorname{Inv}(\sigma):=\{(i,j)\in n\times n:i<j\text{ and }\sigma(i)>\sigma(j)\},\qquad \operatorname{inv}(\sigma):=|\operatorname{Inv}(\sigma)|.$$

The **sign** of $\sigma$ is the integer

$$\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma):=(-1)^{\operatorname{inv}(\sigma)}\in\{+1,-1\}.$$

The permutation is **even** when its sign is $+1$, equivalently when its
inversion number is even, and **odd** when its sign is $-1$, equivalently when
its inversion number is odd. For $n=0$ or $n=1$, every inversion set is empty,
so the unique permutation is even.

Let $(S,m)$ be a finite Coxeter matrix with presented group $W$, length $\ell$ and geometric representation $\sigma:W\to\mathrm{GL}_K(E)$ as in [[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]], [[def-hh-geometric-coxeter-representation-and-roots]] and [[lem-hh-dihedral-root-recurrence-and-root-sign]], and let $J\subseteq S$.

1. **Support and reduction.** For every $w\in W$ the set $S(w)$ of letters occurring in a reduced expression of $w$ is independent of the reduced expression, and every word in $S$ representing $w$ can be transformed into a reduced expression by repeatedly deleting two letters (Tits reduction, using only letters already present). Consequently
$$W_J=\langle J\rangle=\{w\in W:S(w)\subseteq J\}.$$
2. **Intrinsic parabolic presentation.** Let $W_J^\ast$ be the group presented by the restricted Coxeter matrix $(J,m|_J)$ in the sense of [[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]]. The canonical homomorphism $W_J^\ast\to W_J$, $s\mapsto s$, is an isomorphism. Hence $(W_J,J)$ is a Coxeter system, its intrinsic length function $\ell_J$ agrees with the ambient length $\ell$ on $W_J$, and $W_J\cap S=J$.
3. **Minimal coset representatives.** Every right coset $W_J a:=\{ua:u\in W_J\}$ ($a\in W$, [[def-coset]]) has a unique element $d$ of minimal length; it is characterized by $\ell(sd)>\ell(d)$ for all $s\in J$, and it satisfies
$$\ell(ud)=\ell(u)+\ell(d)\qquad\text{for all }u\in W_J .$$
Equivalently, every $w\in W$ has a unique factorization $w=u\,d$ with $u\in W_J$ and $d$ the minimal representative of the right coset $W_J d$, and then $\ell(w)=\ell(u)+\ell(d)$. By inversion ($w\mapsto w^{-1}$ preserves lengths and interchanges the two coset families $\{W_Ja\}$ and $\{aW_J\}$), every left coset $aW_J:=\{au:u\in W_J\}$ has a unique minimal element $d$, characterized by $\ell(ds)>\ell(d)$ for all $s\in J$ and satisfying $\ell(du)=\ell(d)+\ell(u)$ for all $u\in W_J$.
4. **Type A.** Let $n\ge2$, $S=\{s_1,\dots,s_{n-1}\}$ and $m(s_i,s_j):=3$ if $|i-j|=1$, $m(s_i,s_j):=2$ if $|i-j|>1$ (a Coxeter matrix of type $A_{n-1}$). Then $s_i\mapsto(i\ i+1)$ extends to an isomorphism $W\to S_n$ (the letters $1,\dots,n$ carry the library's symmetric group by the order-preserving identification with $\{0,\dots,n-1\}$, under which $(i\ i+1)$ is the adjacent transposition $(i-1\ i)$), and for every $w\in W$,
$$\ell(w)=\operatorname{inv}\bigl(\varphi(w)\bigr),$$
the inversion number of the corresponding permutation ([[def-inversions-inversion-number-and-sign]]). In particular a word in the $s_i$ is reduced if and only if its length equals the inversion number of its value.

Let $(S,m)$ be a finite Coxeter matrix, let $W$ be the presented group with
length function $\ell$ ([[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]]), and
let $T=\{wsw^{-1}:w\in W,\ s\in S\}$ be the set of reflections of $W$
([[def-cg-canonical-reflection-homomorphism]]). Throughout, $I$ and $J$ denote
subsets of $S$.

**(1) Standard parabolic subgroups.** For $I\subseteq S$ put

$$W_I:=\langle s:s\in I\rangle\le W,$$

the subgroup generated by $I$ ([[def-generated-subgroup]]); $W_I$ is the
**standard parabolic subgroup** of $(W,S)$ of type $I$. Thus
$W_\emptyset=\{1\}$ and $W_S=W$. By
[[thm-hh-parabolic-minimal-representatives-and-length-additivity]] (1),(2): for
every $w\in W$ one has $w\in W_I$ if and only if $S(w)\subseteq I$, where
$S(w)$ is the (well-defined) set of letters of any reduced expression of $w$;
$(W_I,I)$ is a Coxeter system; its intrinsic length function agrees with
$\ell|_{W_I}$; and $W_I\cap S=I$.

**(2) Descents and the one-sided quotients.** For $w\in W$ put

$$D_L(w):=\{s\in S:\ell(sw)<\ell(w)\},\qquad D_R(w):=\{s\in S:\ell(ws)<\ell(w)\};$$

each of $\ell(sw)-\ell(w)$ and $\ell(ws)-\ell(w)$ lies in $\{\pm1\}$
([[thm-hh-coxeter-exchange-deletion-and-faithfulness]] (1)). Define

$$W^I:=\{w\in W:\ell(ws)>\ell(w)\text{ for all }s\in I\}=\{w\in W:D_R(w)\cap I=\emptyset\},$$

$${}^IW:=\{w\in W:\ell(sw)>\ell(w)\text{ for all }s\in I\}=\{w\in W:D_L(w)\cap I=\emptyset\}.$$

Conventions are fixed here: in ${}^IW$ the subset $I$ is tested on the left, in
$W^I$ it is tested on the right; $\ell(sw)$ means left multiplication by $s$
and $\ell(ws)$ right multiplication. The interpretation of these sets as sets
of coset representatives is not part of the definition; it is quoted from
[[thm-hh-parabolic-minimal-representatives-and-length-additivity]] (3) and
re-examined in [[thm-cg-parabolic-intersections-and-coset-factorization]] (3):
every $w\in W$ has a unique factorization

$$w=u\,d\qquad(u\in W_I,\ d\in{}^IW),\qquad \ell(w)=\ell(u)+\ell(d),$$

where $d$ is the unique element of minimal length in the right coset $W_Iw$, and
it satisfies $\ell(ud)=\ell(u)+\ell(d)$ for all $u\in W_I$; symmetrically every
$w\in W$ has a unique factorization

$$w=d\,v\qquad(d\in W^I,\ v\in W_I),\qquad \ell(w)=\ell(d)+\ell(v),$$

where $d$ is the unique element of minimal length in the left coset $wW_I$, and
it satisfies $\ell(dv)=\ell(d)+\ell(v)$ for all $v\in W_I$. Thus ${}^IW$
consists exactly of the elements of minimal length in the right cosets
$W_Iw=\{uw:u\in W_I\}$ and $W^I$ consists exactly of the elements of minimal
length in the sets $wW_I=\{wv:v\in W_I\}$. Inversion gives
$W^I=({}^IW)^{-1}$, because $\ell(x)=\ell(x^{-1})$ and $(sw)^{-1}=w^{-1}s$.

**(3) The two-sided quotients.** Define

$${}^IW^J:={}^IW\cap W^J=\{w\in W:\ell(sw)>\ell(w)\text{ for all }s\in I\ \text{ and }\ \ell(ws)>\ell(w)\text{ for all }s\in J\};$$

thus ${}^\emptyset W^J=W^J$, ${}^IW^\emptyset={}^IW$ and ${}^\emptyset
W^\emptyset=W$, and the members of ${}^IW^J$ are exactly the elements of $W$
with no left descent in $I$ and no right descent in $J$. Whether ${}^IW^J$ is a
set of representatives of the double cosets $W_IwW_J$ is again a theorem, not a
definition; it is proved in
[[thm-cg-double-coset-unique-minimum-and-normal-form]].

**(4) Parabolic subgroups and reflection subgroups.** A subgroup $H\le W$ is a
**parabolic subgroup** of $(W,S)$ if

$$H=wW_Iw^{-1}\qquad\text{for some }w\in W,\ I\subseteq S;$$

a parabolic subgroup with $w=1$ is *standard*. A subgroup $H\le W$ is a
**reflection subgroup** if $H=\langle H\cap T\rangle$, i.e. if $H$ is generated
by the reflections it contains. Every parabolic subgroup is a reflection
subgroup, since $wW_Iw^{-1}=\langle wsw^{-1}:s\in I\rangle$ and
$wsw^{-1}\in T$ for all $s\in S$, $w\in W$. No converse is asserted: it is not
claimed here that a subgroup generated by reflections is parabolic, and the
companion examples page computes test cases for the two distinctions created by
this definition --- standard parabolic versus parabolic, and reflection subgroup
versus parabolic subgroup.

derivations.claim: **The bases.** The $A$-span of $\{H_u:u\in W_J\}$ is exactly $H_J$: it contains the generators and is closed under their left and right multiplication by the quadratic multiplication rule, while every $H_u$ is a reduced product of generators in $J$. By [F1], the standard basis partitions as $\{H_uH_y:u\in W_J,\ y\in{}^JW\}$. Hence multiplication is an isomorphism of left $H_J$-modules $\bigoplus_{y\in{}^JW}H_J\to H_v(n)$, $(h_y)_y\mapsto\sum_yh_yH_y$: expanding each $h_y$ in the independent $H_u$ proves injectivity and the unique factorization proves surjectivity. Tensoring this isomorphism with either character module $A$ gives $A\otimes_{H_J}H_v(n)\cong\bigoplus_{y\in{}^JW}A$. The images of the coordinate generators are $m_y$, respectively $n_y$, proving both bases.

**The two minimal branches.** Let $x\in{}^JW$, $s\in S$ and suppose $xs\in{}^JW$. Since $xs=(xsx^{-1})x$ is the left translate of $x$ by a transposition and $\ell(xs)=\ell(x)\pm1$, [F4] shows that $xs>x$ holds exactly when $\ell(xs)=\ell(x)+1$, and $xs<x$ exactly when $\ell(xs)=\ell(x)-1$. If $xs>x$ then [F2] gives $H_xH_s=H_{xs}$, so by step 1.1 and the module structure $m_xC_s=1\otimes(H_{xs}+vH_x)=m_{xs}+v\,m_x$, and likewise $n_xC_s=n_{xs}+v\,n_x$. If $xs<x$ then $H_xH_s=H_{xs}+(v^{-1}-v)H_x$, so $m_xC_s=m_{xs}+(v^{-1}-v)m_x+v\,m_x=m_{xs}+v^{-1}m_x$, and likewise $n_xC_s=n_{xs}+v^{-1}n_x$.

**The parabolic property.** Let $x\in{}^JW$ and $s=s_j$, and suppose $xs\notin{}^JW$; by [F5] $xs$ has a left descent in $J$: some $r\in J$ has $r+1$ to the left of $r$ in $xs$. Since $x\in{}^JW$ has no such descent, while $xs$ differs from $x$ only by the swap of the entries at positions $j$ and $j+1$, the only changed relative order is that of the values $a:=x(j)$, $b:=x(j+1)$, so $\{r,r+1\}=\{a,b\}$. The order $a=r+1$, $b=r$ is excluded because it would already be a left descent of $x$. Hence $a=r$ and $b=r+1$ with $r\in J$; the two permutations $xs$ and $s_rx$ coincide because both are obtained from $x$ by interchanging the values $r$ and $r+1$. Moreover $\ell(s_rx)>\ell(x)$ because $r\in J$ and $x\in{}^JW$, so $\ell(xs)=\ell(x)+1$ and $xs>x$ by [F4](a),(b); thus $H_xH_s=H_{xs}=H_{s_rx}=H_rH_x$ by [F1] and [F2]. Therefore $m_xC_s=1\otimes(H_{xs}+vH_x)=\varphi_+(H_r)m_x+v\,m_x=(v^{-1}+v)m_x$ and $n_xC_s=\varphi_-(H_r)n_x+v\,n_x=(-v+v)n_x=0$. Uniqueness of $r$ holds because $r$ is the value whose swap produces $xs$; this proves (4) and the third branch of (2).

**The bar descent.** The map $\beta(a\otimes h):=\bar a\otimes\bar h$ is well defined on $A\otimes_{H_J}H_v(n)$: it suffices to check $\overline{a\varphi_\pm(t)}\otimes\bar h=\bar a\otimes\overline{th}$ for $t=H_s$, $s\in J$, where the left side is $\bar a\,\overline{\varphi_\pm(H_s)}\otimes\bar h$ and the right side is $\bar a\otimes\overline{H_s}\bar h=\bar a\otimes(H_s-(v^{-1}-v))\bar h=\bar a\,\varphi_\pm(H_s-(v^{-1}-v))\otimes\bar h$, and $\varphi_+(H_s-(v^{-1}-v))=v^{-1}+(v-v^{-1})=v=\overline{v^{-1}}$, $\varphi_-(H_s-(v^{-1}-v))=-v+(v-v^{-1})=-v^{-1}=\overline{-v}$ by [F3]; multiplicativity extends this to all $t$. The map is $A$-antilinear, involutive ($\beta^2=\mathrm{id}$ because bar is an involution on $A$ and on $H_v(n)$), and satisfies $\beta(X\cdot h')=\beta(X)\cdot\overline{h'}$ because $(a\otimes h)\cdot h'=a\otimes hh'$ maps to $\bar a\otimes\overline{hh'}=\bar a\otimes\bar h\bar h'=(\bar a\otimes\bar h)\cdot\bar h'$.

**Triangular expansion and top coefficient.** For $x=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_k}$ reduced, [F3] gives $\overline{H_x}=\prod_{m=1}^k(H_{s_{i_m}}-(v^{-1}-v))$. The term choosing every generator is $H_x$. Every other term is a scalar times a product of fewer than $k$ generators selected from this word. Successive use of [F2] expands such a product into $H_z$ whose group labels are products of subwords of the selected word: each multiplication retains the old label or appends the current generator. Deletion of pairs in [F4] reduces each such group word to a reduced subword of the original reduced expression for $x$. Thus $z\le x$, and $\ell(z)<k$ because at most $k-1$ letters were retained, so $z<x$. Consequently $\overline{H_x}=H_x+\sum_{z<x}c_zH_z$. For each $z<x$ factor $z=uy$ length-additively with $u\in W_J$, $y\in{}^JW$. A reduced expression of $z$ contains a reduced suffix for $y$, so $y\le z<x$. In either module $1\otimes H_z=\varphi_\pm(H_u)(1\otimes H_y)$. Applying the bar from step 2.3 therefore gives exactly the triangular expansions in (3), with top coefficient one and all lower coefficients in $A$.
Parts (1), (2), (3) and (4) are proved in steps 1.1, 2.1 together with 2.2, 2.3 together with 3.1, and 2.2 respectively.

risk_review.notes: The span of H_u for u in W_J is the subalgebra, and the standard basis partitions into a free left H_J basis, proving tensor independence. Adjacent-position swapping can disrupt only one consecutive-value pair inside a J block, giving xs=s_r x with an ascent. All three action branches and both bar-balancing scalar identities follow. Quadratic multiplication expands nonreduced subwords; pair deletion makes their labels reduced subwords below x, so the bar top coefficient is one. J=empty/full and n=1 are valid; no AC.

citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), inherited from the
published block theory. Work in category $\mathcal O$ of a finite-dimensional
complex semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ with Cartan $\mathfrak h$,
positive system $\Phi^+$, simple roots $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_r$, Weyl group
$W$, Weyl vector $\rho$ and dot action $w\cdot\lambda=w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho$, as
in [[def-bgg-category-o]] and
[[def-dot-action-facets-and-single-wall-translation-data]].

**(1) Dot-antidominant integral weights.** A weight $\mu$ is **dot-antidominant**
if $\langle\mu+\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle\le0$ for every $\alpha\in\Phi^+$, and
**integral** if $\langle\mu,\alpha_i^\vee\rangle\in\mathbb Z$ for all $i$
([[def-integral-weyl-group-of-a-weight]],
[[def-integral-dominant-and-strictly-dominant-weights]]).

**(2) The dot stabilizer.** Fix such a weight $\mu$ and put
$$J=J(\mu):=\{i:\langle\mu+\rho,\alpha_i^\vee\rangle=0\},\qquad W_\mu:=W_J=\langle s_i:i\in J\rangle.$$
Then the dot stabilizer $\{v\in W:v\cdot\mu=\mu\}$ equals $W_J$. Indeed, for
$i\in J$ the reflection $s_i$ fixes $\mu+\rho$, so $W_J$ lies in the
stabilizer; conversely the stabilizer of an integral dot-antidominant weight
is generated by the reflections it contains and is a standard parabolic
([[lem-finite-weyl-closed-chambers-and-stabilizers]], applied to the dominant
vector $-\mu-\rho$), and by
[[def-cg-parabolic-quotient-and-two-sided-minima]] a standard parabolic
subgroup is $W_I$ for the set $I$ of simple reflections it contains, which is
exactly $J$. In particular $w'\cdot\mu=w\cdot\mu$ if and only if
$w^{-1}w'\in W_J$, that is, $w'\in wW_J$.

**(3) The singular integral block.** The **singular integral block**
$\mathcal O_\mu$ is the block of
[[thm-central-character-summands-split-into-linkage-blocks]] of the central
character $\chi_\mu$ of $\mu$; by
[[cor-central-characters-are-dot-weyl-orbits]] two central characters agree
exactly when the highest weights lie in one dot orbit, and by
[[thm-category-o-decomposes-by-generalized-central-character]] the block is a
summand of $\mathcal O$. Its simple objects $L(w\cdot\mu)$, standard objects
$\Delta(w\cdot\mu)=M(w\cdot\mu)$, costandard objects $\nabla(w\cdot\mu)$ and
projective covers $P(w\cdot\mu)$ are indexed by $w\in W$
([[def-standard-and-costandard-objects-in-category-o]],
[[def-verma-module]]); by (2) the label $w\cdot\mu$ depends only on the coset
$wW_J$, so the labels can be normalized by the minimal right coset
representatives

$$W^J=\{w\in W:\ell(ws)>\ell(w)\ \text{for all }s\in J\},$$

which are exactly the elements of minimal length in the cosets $wW_J$
([[thm-hh-parabolic-minimal-representatives-and-length-additivity]] (3));
inversion carries $W^J$ onto the minimal left coset representatives ${}^JW$,
and the two families are the label sets of the parabolic Hecke modules of
[[def-parabolic-hecke-module-and-antispherical-standard-basis]].

**(4) Highest-weight structure and multiplicities.** The block is a
highest-weight category: it has enough projectives
([[thm-category-o-has-enough-projectives]]), projective covers have finite
Verma flags ([[thm-projectives-in-category-o-have-verma-flags]]), the standard
classes and simple classes are bases of the Grothendieck group
([[def-grothendieck-group-and-character-of-category-o]],
[[prop-the-grothendieck-group-of-o-has-simple-and-standard-bases]]), and it
satisfies BGG reciprocity
$$(P(w\cdot\mu):\Delta(y\cdot\mu))=[M(y\cdot\mu):L(w\cdot\mu)]$$
([[thm-bgg-reciprocity]], [[def-verma-flag-and-its-multiplicities]]). The
multiplicity matrix is unitriangular for the refinement of the dominance order
on the dot orbit: $(P(w\cdot\mu):\Delta(w\cdot\mu))=1$, and
$(P(w\cdot\mu):\Delta(y\cdot\mu))\neq0$ only if $y\cdot\mu\ge w\cdot\mu$
([[cor-projective-standard-labels-lie-above-the-head]]); the ordinary
standard/costandard Hom and $\mathrm{Ext}^1$ vanishing used on this page is
[[lem-standard-costandard-hom-and-ext-vanishing]].

**(5) Regular versus singular.** The block is **regular** when $J=\varnothing$
(the weight lies on no wall) and **singular** when $J\neq\varnothing$; the
singular translation statements of this page use this notation, and
$J=\varnothing$ recovers the regular case. The genuine regular-parabolic
multiplicity statements below have their own separate explicit dominant
regular base and are not consequences of the notation here.

Every $W$-orbit in $E$ has exactly one point in $\overline{\mathcal C}$. For $\eta\in\overline{\mathcal C}$, its stabilizer is generated by those simple reflections $s_i$ with $(\eta,\alpha_i)=0$. The group acts simply transitively on open chambers. There is a unique longest element $w_0$, characterized by $w_0\Phi^+=\Phi^-$; it has length $|\Phi^+|$ and satisfies $w_0^2=1$. In particular every weight orbit has a unique dominant weight. These assertions include rank zero and singular wall points, without AC.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Fix a finite-dimensional
complex semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$, a Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$,
and a positive Borel $\mathfrak b=\mathfrak h\oplus\mathfrak n^+$, with the
chosen positive system $\Phi^+$ and Weyl vector $\rho$ of
[[def-weyl-vector-rho-for-a-chosen-positive-system]] and Weyl group $W$ acting
by the root reflections
$s_\alpha(\lambda)=\lambda-\lambda(\alpha^\vee)\alpha$ of
[[def-root-reflections-and-the-weyl-group-action]]. Write the dot action as
$w\mathbin\cdot\lambda=w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho$ and write
$\langle\zeta,\alpha^\vee\rangle$ for the pairing with the coroot
([[thm-the-root-set-is-a-reduced-crystallographic-root-system]]).

Put $R=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\Phi\subseteq\mathfrak h^*$. For a weight
$\lambda\in R$, the **dot-Weyl facet** of $\lambda$ is
the set of weights
$$F_\lambda=\{\zeta\in R:\ \operatorname{sgn}\langle\zeta+\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle=\operatorname{sgn}\langle\lambda+\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle\ \text{for every root }\alpha\in\Phi\},$$
where $\operatorname{sgn}$ takes the values positive, zero and negative. Its
**upper closure** is
$$F_\lambda^+=\{\zeta\in R:\ \langle\zeta+\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle\ \text{is positive, zero or nonpositive according as}\ \langle\lambda+\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle\ \text{is positive, zero or negative, for every }\alpha\in\Phi^+\}.$$
The upper-closure test uses only positive roots: imposing it also on their
negatives would incorrectly exclude wall points from the upper closure of
the antidominant chamber. Thus $F_\lambda\subseteq F_\lambda^+$, the facets refine the closures of the
open Weyl chambers, and $F_\lambda$ depends only on the wall-sign pattern of
$\lambda+\rho$.

Two special positions are used throughout. A weight $\lambda$ is **dot-regular**
when $\langle\lambda+\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle\neq0$ for every root $\alpha$, so
that $F_\lambda$ is an open chamber; it is **dot-antidominant** when
$\langle\lambda+\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle\le0$ for every positive root $\alpha$.
Integrality of weights is the notion of
[[def-integral-dominant-and-strictly-dominant-weights]].

A **single-wall translation datum** is a triple $(\lambda,\mu,\alpha)$
consisting of integral dot-antidominant weights $\lambda,\mu$ and a positive
root $\alpha$ such that:

1. $\lambda$ is dot-regular, so $F_\lambda$ is an open chamber;
2. $\mu+\rho$ lies in the closure of the chamber of $\lambda+\rho$: one has
   $\langle\mu+\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle=0$, and
   $\langle\mu+\rho,\beta^\vee\rangle$ has the same sign as
   $\langle\lambda+\rho,\beta^\vee\rangle$ for every root $\beta$ different
   from $\alpha$ and from its multiples;
3. the dot stabilizer $S_\mu:=\{w\in W:w\mathbin\cdot\mu=\mu\}$ is exactly $\{1,s_\alpha\}$.

Equivalently, $F_\mu$ is a codimension-one facet in the closure of the open
antidominant chamber $F_\lambda$, with $S_\mu=\{1,s_\alpha\}$.
This dot stabilizer and the integral-reflection group $W_\mu$ of
[[def-integral-weyl-group-of-a-weight]] are defined by different conditions:
since $\mu$ is integral, all simple reflections belong to $W_\mu$, so
$W_\mu=W$, whereas $S_\mu=\{1,s_\alpha\}$. The groups coincide in rank one
and differ when the rank is greater than one. In
this datum the **translating weight** $\nu$ is the unique dominant weight of
the linear Weyl orbit $W(\mu-\lambda)$; it exists and is unique by
[[lem-finite-weyl-closed-chambers-and-stabilizers]], and it is integral because
$\mu-\lambda$ is integral and $W$ preserves the weight lattice. The **wall
reflection** is $s:=s_\alpha$.

The basic example is $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ with the datum
$(\lambda,\mu)=(-2,-1)$: here $\rho=1$, $\mu=-\rho$,
$\lambda+\rho=-1$ spans the open negative chamber, $\mu+\rho=0$ is the single
wall, and the dot-stabilizer of $\mu$ is $\{1,s\}$. The pair $(0,-1)$ uses the dominant regular representative rather than the
antidominant representative required here. It defines the same translation
functors: $0$ and $-2$ have the same central character, and both weight
differences have dominant representative $1$ with translating module
$L(1)$, which is self-dual. These functors are defined in
the next definition on this page.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\nu$ be a dominant
integral weight
([[def-integral-dominant-and-strictly-dominant-weights]]) and let $\gamma$ be
a weight of the finite-dimensional simple module $L(\nu)$
([[thm-finite-dimensional-simple-modules-are-classified-by-dominant-highest-weights]]).
Then, in the $W$-invariant positive definite form on the real span $E$ of the
roots ([[prop-the-roots-form-a-reduced-crystallographic-euclidean-root-system]]),
$$\lvert\gamma\rvert\le\lvert\nu\rvert,$$
with equality if and only if $\gamma$ lies in the Weyl orbit $W\nu$; moreover
every weight in $W\nu$ occurs in $L(\nu)$ with multiplicity one.

Every $W$-orbit in $E$ has exactly one point in $\overline{\mathcal C}$. For $\eta\in\overline{\mathcal C}$, its stabilizer is generated by those simple reflections $s_i$ with $(\eta,\alpha_i)=0$. The group acts simply transitively on open chambers. There is a unique longest element $w_0$, characterized by $w_0\Phi^+=\Phi^-$; it has length $|\Phi^+|$ and satisfies $w_0^2=1$. In particular every weight orbit has a unique dominant weight. These assertions include rank zero and singular wall points, without AC.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Work in the real span
$E$ of the roots with its $W$-invariant positive definite form, and let $\xi$
and $\eta$ be weights in $E$ that are dominant, so
$\langle\xi,\alpha_i^\vee\rangle\ge0$ and
$\langle\eta,\alpha_i^\vee\rangle\ge0$ for every simple root $\alpha_i$
([[def-integral-dominant-and-strictly-dominant-weights]]). Then
$$\lvert\xi-w\eta\rvert\ge\lvert\xi-\eta\rvert\qquad\text{for every }w\in W,$$
and equality holds if and only if $w\eta$ lies in the set
$W_\xi\eta=\{v\eta:v\in W_\xi\}$, where $W_\xi=\{v\in W:v\xi=\xi\}$ is the
stabilizer of $\xi$. In particular, if $\xi$ is regular, so that
$W_\xi=\{1\}$, then equality forces $w\eta=\eta$; if $\xi=0$ then equality
holds for every $w$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $E$ be a
finite-dimensional $\mathfrak h$-semisimple $\mathfrak g$-module with weight
multiplicities $\dim E_\eta$
([[def-weight-and-weight-space-of-a-lie-algebra-representation]]). For every
weight $\mu$, the object $E\otimes\Delta(\mu)$ has a finite Verma flag
([[def-verma-flag-and-its-multiplicities]]) whose factors are $\Delta(\mu+\eta)$,
the factor $\Delta(\mu+\eta)$ occurring $\dim E_\eta$ times; the factors can be
ordered so that a real-linear height $\ell$ with $\ell(\alpha_i)=1$ is nonincreasing.

Consequently, if $X\in\mathcal O$ has a finite Verma flag with multiplicities
$(X:\Delta(\nu))$, then $E\otimes X$ has a finite Verma flag and
$$(E\otimes X:\Delta(\mu))=\sum_\eta\dim E_\eta\,(X:\Delta(\mu-\eta)).$$

For a finite-dimensional complex Lie algebra $\mathfrak a$, its **universal enveloping algebra** is $U(\mathfrak a)=T(\mathfrak a)/(xy-yx-[x,y])$, where $T$ is the algebra of finite linear combinations of finite tensor words, including the empty word $1$, and the denominator is the two-sided ideal generated by the displayed relations. For any ordered finite basis $x_1,\ldots,x_n$, the monomials $x_1^{a_1}\cdots x_n^{a_n}$ form a vector-space basis of $U(\mathfrak a)$.

Now let $\mathfrak g$ be finite-dimensional complex semisimple with a Cartan and positive system as in the preceding root-structure lemma. Set $\mathfrak n^\pm=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\Phi^\pm}\mathfrak g_\alpha$ and $\mathfrak b=\mathfrak h\oplus\mathfrak n^+$. For $\lambda\in\mathfrak h^*$ let $\mathbb C_\lambda$ be the one-dimensional $\mathfrak b$-module on which $\mathfrak h$ acts by $\lambda$ and $\mathfrak n^+$ by zero, and define $M(\lambda)=U(\mathfrak g)\otimes_{U(\mathfrak b)}\mathbb C_\lambda$. It is generated by $v_\lambda=1\otimes1$, with $hv_\lambda=\lambda(h)v_\lambda$ and $\mathfrak n^+v_\lambda=0$, and is universal for these relations. Its negative-root ordered monomials on $v_\lambda$ form a basis; its support is $\lambda-Q_+$, each weight space is finite-dimensional and the top space has dimension one. It has a unique simple quotient $L(\lambda)$.

For every dominant integral $\lambda$, $L(\lambda)$ is finite-dimensional, its support is contained in $\lambda-Q_+$, its top weight has multiplicity one, and all its weight multiplicities are $W$-invariant. Every nonzero finite-dimensional simple $\mathfrak g$-module is exactly one such $L(\lambda)$ up to isomorphism, with a unique dominant integral highest weight. These assertions include the zero algebra and use no AC.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra with Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$, a chosen positive-root system and corresponding Borel, Weyl group $W$, and half-sum $\rho$ of positive roots. Let $\chi_\lambda$ and $\chi_\mu$ be the central characters obtained from highest weights $\lambda,\mu\in\mathfrak h^*$ for this Borel. Then

$$\chi_\lambda=\chi_\mu \quad \text{if and only if} \quad \mu\in W\cdot \lambda,$$

where $W\cdot \lambda:=\{w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho : w\in W\}$.

derivations.claim: Let $w,w'\in W$ and let $\gamma$ be a weight of $E$ with $w'\mathbin\cdot\mu=w\mathbin\cdot\lambda+\gamma$. Since $w'\mathbin\cdot\mu-[w\mathbin\cdot\lambda]=w'(\mu_\bullet)-w(\lambda_\bullet)$, setting $x=(w')^{-1}w$ gives $x\lambda_\bullet=\mu_\bullet-(w')^{-1}\gamma$, that is, $(w')^{-1}\gamma=\mu_\bullet-x\lambda_\bullet$.

By [F2] one has $\lvert\gamma\rvert\le\lvert\nu\rvert=\lvert\mu_\bullet-\lambda_\bullet\rvert$, and $W$-invariance of the form gives $\lvert(w')^{-1}\gamma\rvert=\lvert\gamma\rvert$, so the identity of step 1.1 yields $\lvert\mu_\bullet-x\lambda_\bullet\rvert\le\lvert\mu_\bullet-\lambda_\bullet\rvert$. On the other hand [F3] applied to the dominant vectors $\xi=-\mu_\bullet$ and $\eta=-\lambda_\bullet$ (dominant and regular by [F1]) gives $\lvert\mu_\bullet-\lambda_\bullet\rvert=\lvert\xi-\eta\rvert\le\lvert\xi-x\eta\rvert=\lvert\mu_\bullet-x\lambda_\bullet\rvert$.

The two inequalities of step 2.1 are equalities, so the equality case of [F3] applies: $x\eta\in\operatorname{Stab}_W(\xi)\eta$, and $\operatorname{Stab}_W(\xi)=W_J$ by [F1], that is, $x(-\lambda_\bullet)\in W_J(-\lambda_\bullet)$. Choose $u\in W_J$ with $x\lambda_\bullet=u\lambda_\bullet$; then $u^{-1}x$ fixes the regular vector $\lambda_\bullet$, so $u^{-1}x=1$ and $x=u\in W_J$. Since $W_J$ is the dot stabilizer of $\mu$ by [F1], $x\mathbin\cdot\mu=\mu$, and therefore $w'\mathbin\cdot\mu=w\mathbin\cdot(x\mathbin\cdot\mu)=w\mathbin\cdot\mu$. Moreover $\gamma=w'\mathbin\cdot\mu-w\mathbin\cdot\lambda=w\mathbin\cdot\mu-w\mathbin\cdot\lambda=w(\mu-\lambda)$. Finally $\lvert\gamma\rvert=\lvert\mu_\bullet-\lambda_\bullet\rvert=\lvert\nu\rvert$ and $\gamma=w(\mu-\lambda)\in W(\mu-\lambda)=W\nu$, so by [F2] the weight $\gamma$ occurs in $E$ with multiplicity one.

For the reformulation, fix $w$ and let $\eta$ be a weight in the dot orbit of $\mu$, so $\eta=w'\mathbin\cdot\mu$ for some $w'$ and $\eta$ has the central character of $\mu$ by [F5]. If $\dim E_{\eta-w\mathbin\cdot\lambda}\ne0$, then $\gamma:=\eta-w\mathbin\cdot\lambda$ is a weight of $E$ with $w'\mathbin\cdot\mu=w\mathbin\cdot\lambda+\gamma$, so step 3.1 gives $\eta=w'\mathbin\cdot\mu=w\mathbin\cdot\mu$ and $\gamma=w(\mu-\lambda)$; conversely $\dim E_{w(\mu-\lambda)}=1$ by step 3.1. Hence among labels with the central character of $\mu$ only $\Delta(w\mathbin\cdot\mu)$ occurs, with multiplicity one, in the Verma flag of $E\otimes\Delta(w\mathbin\cdot\lambda)$ supplied by [F4].

Steps 3.1 and 4.1 prove both formulations: the tensor-weight identity forces $w'\mathbin\cdot\mu=w\mathbin\cdot\mu$ and $\gamma=w(\mu-\lambda)$ with multiplicity one, and the only Verma factor of $E\otimes\Delta(w\mathbin\cdot\lambda)$ with central character $\chi_\mu$ is $\Delta(w\mathbin\cdot\mu)$, once.

boundaries.evidence: For J=empty the stabilizer is trivial and step 3.1 forces x=1. For a single-wall J={s}, the argument specializes to the published single-wall exclusion; the regular case is not a single-wall datum.

The proof is the equality case of the norm bound |gamma| <= |nu|; the zero-distance case mu = lambda makes gamma = 0 and w' . mu = w . mu, exactly what the squeeze returns, so the vanishing-distance case is covered rather than excluded. See the Statement and the numbered verification steps.
Step 3.1 proves that the retained tensor weight is extremal and has multiplicity one; step 4.1 gives the unique projected standard. For W_J={1}, the same squeeze applies with trivial stabilizer.
J=empty is a regular target; lambda=mu gives nu=0, E trivial and gamma=0; J=S gives mu=-rho. All are covered by the same norm squeeze in steps 2.1–4.1.

lambda and mu are dot-antidominant, the endpoints of their dot orbits, and the hypothesis F_mu subseteq closure(F_lambda) is itself an endpoint-closure relation between facets. See the Statement and the numbered verification steps.

The Axiom of Choice is declared and inherited from the classification and norm-bound suppliers; the only selection is the dominant representative nu of the finite orbit W(mu-lambda), which is unique. See the Statement and the numbered verification steps.

boundaries.reason: There is no biconditional in the Statement; the exclusion implication is proved in steps 1.1–3.1 and the multiplicity reformulation in step 4.1.
No converse is asserted: the statement is a one-directional exclusion/uniqueness statement, so there is no reverse implication to verify.

risk_review.notes: Transporting the tensor-weight equality gives gamma norm at most the translating extremal norm. Dominant distance comparison gives the opposite inequality; equality and regularity force x=(w-prime)^(-1)w into W_J. Thus the two singular labels coincide and the extremal weight has multiplicity one. Tensor flags and central-character orbits supply exactly the claimed factor; the converse weight exists because w(mu-lambda) lies in W nu. mu=-rho and J=empty behave correctly. AC is inherited, with no new infinite selection.

boundaries.evidence: J=empty gives p=b and ordinary O. For J=S, p=g and u=0: radical nilpotence is vacuous, but Levi local finiteness is not. Finite generation then makes every object finite dimensional. See the Definition and local-finiteness remark.

Setting u_J . E(lambda) = 0 defines the p-module structure on E(lambda), and local finiteness says every vector is annihilated by a power of the nilpotent u_J; these two zero-actions are the exact content of (2) and (3). See the Definition.

The generalized Verma has a one-dimensional highest-weight line and the unique simple head L(lambda); the head itself need not be one dimensional. See Definition (4) and the Verma-head supplier in the Remarks.

The extreme cases J = empty (recovering ordinary category O) and J = S (finite-dimensional semisimple objects) are included; non-semisimple centre z_J for intermediate J is handled through the grading element zeta of the Levi definition.

boundaries.reason: Dominance in (1) is a pointwise coroot-pairing condition, and no order intervals or limiting processes are taken in the definition.

boundaries.evidence: The Axiom of Choice is declared and inherited from the published category-O and Levi-module suppliers (projective covers, Weyl complete reducibility); no new choice principle is introduced. See the Definition.

The characterization in (3): every vector lies in a finite-dimensional p-submodule implies, by restriction, that it lies in a finite-dimensional l_J-submodule and is killed by a power of u_J; also the "largest quotient" claim of (4) is proved by taking the cyclic finite-dimensional span. See the Definition.

Levi local finiteness and radical local nilpotence yield finite U(p)-spans by PBW. The Remarks prove the equivalent negative-simple-root criterion and Serre closure; no nilpotence of the entire Levi action is required. See Definition (3).

reader_repair.description: Highest vector and ideal stability prove largest quotient; sl2 and finite Levi composition factors prove local finiteness; J=all rank-one duality example.

risk_review.notes: Finite graded PBW pieces are p-stable because positive radical degree raises the zeta eigenvalue and the degree-zero Levi module is killed. A parabolic Verma quotient factors through the finite cyclic Levi simple, since the radical kills its highest vector and its whole Levi span. Local nilpotence of each f_j is equivalent to Levi local finiteness: the sl2 identity forces each simple factor to have dominant integral Levi weight. PBW with the finite radical span proves p-local finiteness, including extensions. Chevalley duality preserves locally finite Levi direct sums. J=empty gives ordinary O; J=S gives finite-dimensional modules, and the corrected sl2 example has M_p(0)=L(0).
