For $\sigma \in S_n$ and $0 \le p,q < n$, define the rank number

$$r_\sigma(p,q) := \big|\{\, i \in n : i \le p \text{ and } \sigma(i)\le q\,\}\big|.$$

For $\sigma,\tau \in S_n$, write

$$\sigma \le_{\mathrm{Bruhat}} \tau \quad:\Longleftrightarrow\quad r_\sigma(p,q)\ge r_\tau(p,q)\ \text{for every }0 \le p,q < n.$$

This is the rank-inequality form of the Bruhat order.

Let $\le$ be the rank-inequality order on the zero-based $S_n$ of [[def-bruhat-order-on-the-symmetric-group]], and identify it with the one-based realization by shifting inputs and values by $1$. (a) This order is the strong Bruhat order of type A: the transitive closure of covers $x\to tx$ where $t$ is a transposition and $\ell(tx)=\ell(x)+1$. (b) If $y\le w$ then $\ell(y)\le\ell(w)$, with equality iff $y=w$; every saturated chain has $\ell(w)-\ell(y)$ steps; and $y\le w$ iff $y^{-1}\le w^{-1}$. (c) $y\le w$ iff for every reduced expression $w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_k}$, $y$ is a reduced subword. (d) For every simple reflection $s$, if $y\le w$ and $\ell(sy)>\ell(y)$, then $y\le sw$; if $y\le w$ and $\ell(sw)<\ell(w)$, then $sy\le w$. (e) Every interval $[y,w]$ is finite; if $y\le w$, then $[y,w]=\{y\}\cup\bigcup_{y\to a\le w}[a,w]$.

Let $n\ge1$ and $A:=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$. For $n\ge2$, define the **normalized type-A Hecke algebra** $H_v(n)$ to be the associative unital $A$-algebra presented by generators $H_{s_1},\ldots,H_{s_{n-1}}$ with relations
$$H_{s_i}^2=1+(v^{-1}-v)H_{s_i},\qquad H_{s_i}H_{s_{i+1}}H_{s_i}=H_{s_{i+1}}H_{s_i}H_{s_{i+1}},\qquad H_{s_i}H_{s_j}=H_{s_j}H_{s_i}\quad(|i-j|>1).$$
For $n=1$, set $H_v(1):=A$.

Here $S_n=\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\ldots,n\})$, $s_i=(i\ i+1)$, and $\ell$ is inversion length as in [[def-symmetric-group]] and [[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]. For $w\in S_n$, let $T_w$ be the standard basis element of the generic Hecke algebra of [[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]], formed from any reduced expression of $w$, and after the coefficient specialization $q\mapsto v^{-2}$ put $H_w:=v^{\ell(w)}T_w$. Equivalently, $H_w=H_{s_{i_1}}\cdots H_{s_{i_k}}$ for a reduced expression $w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_k}$. The standard-basis theorem [[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]] and rescaling by units show that $\{H_w:w\in S_n\}$ is an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$.

Right multiplication by a generator is
$$H_wH_{s_i}=H_{ws_i}\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)+1,\qquad H_wH_{s_i}=H_{ws_i}+(v^{-1}-v)H_w\quad\text{if }\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)-1.$$

**Dictionary with the generic normalization.** If the generic parameter in [[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]] is denoted by $q$, its relation is $T_i^2=(q-1)T_i+q$. The coefficient map $q\mapsto v^{-2}$ is the stated specialization, and $H_{s_i}=vT_i$. This gives $H_{s_i}^2=1+(v^{-1}-v)H_{s_i}$; the braid and commutation relations are unchanged. The two multiplication cases above are the standard-basis rule after the same rescaling.

**Bar assignment.** Let $F$ be the free associative $\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$-algebra on the generator symbols. Define the semilinear algebra map $\iota_0:F\to F$ by $\iota_0(v)=v^{-1}$ and $\iota_0(H_{s_i})=H_{s_i}-(v^{-1}-v)$. In the quotient $H_v(n)$, the quadratic relation makes this latter element the two-sided inverse $H_{s_i}^{-1}$. The next lemma proves that $\iota_0$ preserves the defining ideal and descends to a well-defined involution $\iota$ on $H_v(n)$.

All items on this page use this normalization. It agrees with Elias–Williamson §3.2 under $H_x=v^{\ell(x)}T_x$ and $q=v^{-2}$.

For each $w\in S_n$ there is a unique element $\underline H_w\in H_v(n)$ with (i) $\overline{\underline H_w}=\underline H_w$ and (ii) $\underline H_w\in H_w+\sum_{y<w}v\mathbb Z[v]\,H_y$ (the sum over the lower Bruhat ideal of $w$). The elements $\{\underline H_w\}_{w\in S_n}$ form an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$, and writing $\underline H_w=\sum_{y\le w}p_{y,w}H_y$ one has $p_{w,w}=1$, $p_{y,w}=0$ unless $y\le w$, $p_{y,w}\in v\mathbb Z[v]$ for $y<w$, the bar-duality $p_{x,w}=\sum_{y}r_{x,y}\,\overline{p_{y,w}}$ (matrix form $P=R\bar P$), and the symmetry $p_{y^{-1},w^{-1}}=p_{y,w}$. Moreover for $y<w$, with $d=\ell(w)-\ell(y)$: $p_{y,w}=v^{d}+\text{terms of strictly smaller degree}$ and $p_{y,w}\in v^{d}\,\mathbb Z[v^{-2}]$; in particular every $\underline H_w$ has integer nonnegative coefficients in the standard basis with $p_{y,w}$ of fixed parity $d\bmod 2$.

derivations.claim: **The coefficient matrices.** Define $r_{x,y}\in A$ for $x,y\in{}^JW$ by $\overline{m_y}=\sum_{x\le y}r_{x,y}m_x$, so $r_{x,y}=a_{x,y}$ for $x<y$, $r_{y,y}=1$, and $r_{x,y}=0$ when $x\not\le y$; define $s_{x,y}$ analogously from $\overline{n_y}=\sum_{x\le y}s_{x,y}n_x$. Applying bar to $\overline{m_y}=\sum_{x\le y}r_{x,y}m_x$ and using $\overline{\overline{m_y}}=m_y$ gives $m_y=\sum_{x\le y}\overline{r_{x,y}}\,\overline{m_x}=\sum_{x'\le y}\bigl(\sum_{x:x'\le x\le y}\overline{r_{x,y}}r_{x',x}\bigr)m_{x'}$; by [F1] the coefficient of $m_{x'}$ is $\delta_{x',y}$, that is, $R\bar R=I$ for the unitriangular matrix $R=(r_{x,y})$. A finite unitriangular matrix is invertible, so also $\bar RR=I$; the same identities hold for $S=(s_{x,y})$.

**Construction of the coefficients.** Fix $w\in{}^JW$ and increase $d=\ell(w)-\ell(x)$ over the finite lower ideal $I_w=\{x\in{}^JW:x\le w\}$ of [F3], starting with $c_{w,w}=1$. Suppose $x<w$ and $c_{y,w}$ has been constructed for every $y\in I_w$ with $x<y\le w$, satisfying $c_{y,w}=\sum_{y\le z\le w}r_{y,z}\overline{c_{z,w}}$; note that all cited labels lie in $I_w$. Put $a_x:=\sum_{x<y\le w}r_{x,y}\overline{c_{y,w}}$. Then $\overline{a_x}=\sum_{x<y\le w}\overline{r_{x,y}}c_{y,w}=\sum_{x<y\le z\le w}\overline{r_{x,y}}r_{y,z}\overline{c_{z,w}}=-\sum_{x<z\le w}r_{x,z}\overline{c_{z,w}}=-a_x$, where the middle equality substitutes the induction equations and the third uses $\bar RR=I$ from step 1.1: the sum over $x\le y\le z$ is zero for $x<z$, and its omitted diagonal term is $\overline{r_{x,x}}r_{x,z}=r_{x,z}$. Write $a_x=\sum_{m\in\mathbb Z}\gamma_mv^m$; anti-invariance under $v\mapsto v^{-1}$ gives $\gamma_{-m}=-\gamma_m$, hence $\gamma_0=0$. Define $c_{x,w}:=\sum_{m>0}\gamma_mv^m$, so $c_{x,w}\in v\mathbb Z[v]$ and $c_{x,w}-\overline{c_{x,w}}=a_x$. The induction is finite and uses no choice principle.

**Bar invariance and the coefficient equations.** Set $C_w:=\sum_{y\in I_w}c_{y,w}m_y$. The coefficient of $m_x$ in $\overline{C_w}$ is $\sum_{x\le y\le w}r_{x,y}\overline{c_{y,w}}$. For $x=w$ this is $\overline{c_{w,w}}=1=c_{w,w}$; for $x<w$ it is $\overline{c_{x,w}}+a_x=c_{x,w}$ by step 2.1, and for $x\notin I_w$ the support of $r_{x,y}$ makes the coefficient zero ($x\le y\le w$ would put $x\in I_w$). Hence $\overline{C_w}=C_w$ and the coefficient equation $c_{x,w}=\sum_{x\le y\le w}r_{x,y}\overline{c_{y,w}}$ holds for every $x\le w\in{}^JW$; this proves the existence, the bar invariance and the triangular support $C_w\in m_w+\sum_{y<w}v\mathbb Z[v]m_y$ of (i),(ii). Repeating the identical construction with the matrix $S$ in place of $R$ produces $D_w\in n_w+\sum_{y<w}v\mathbb Z[v]n_y$ with $\overline{D_w}=D_w$.

**Uniqueness.** Suppose $h=\sum_{y<w}c_ym_y\in M^J$ is bar-fixed with every $c_y\in v\mathbb Z[v]$. If $h\ne0$, choose a Bruhat-maximal $x$ in its finite support $I_w\setminus\{w\}$. The coefficient of $m_x$ in $\overline h$ is $\overline{c_x}$: no $y>x$ is supported, and $r_{x,y}\ne0$ requires $x\le y$. Since $h=\overline h$ and the $m_y$ are independent, $c_x=\overline{c_x}$; but bar maps $v\mathbb Z[v]$ into $v^{-1}\mathbb Z[v^{-1}]$, so the common value lies in $v\mathbb Z[v]\cap v^{-1}\mathbb Z[v^{-1}]=\{0\}$ by [F4], a contradiction. Hence $h=0$: the bar-fixed element with the prescribed triangular support is unique, and likewise in $N^J$.

**Bases.** The transition from $(m_x)_{x\in{}^JW}$ to $(C_x)_{x\in{}^JW}$ is unitriangular over the finite Bruhat order (each $C_x=m_x+\sum_{y<x}c_{y,x}m_y$), so it is invertible over $A$; hence $\{C_x\}$ is an $A$-basis of $M^J$. The same holds for $\{D_x\}$ in $N^J$. This proves the theorem for both modules.

boundaries.evidence: Every lower ideal I_w = {x in ^JW : x <= w} is finite and contains w, so no empty index set occurs; the induction starts at the maximal element of I_w. See the Statement and the numbered verification steps.

The uniqueness argument forces the vanishing of any coefficient at a maximal support element via vZ[v] cap v^{-1}Z[v^{-1}] = {0}; genuinely vanishing coefficients are allowed, as n_{e,s_2s_1} = 0 in the companion example shows.
Diagonal coefficient c_{w,w} = 1 initializes the induction of step 2.1, and the unitriangular transition to {C_x} has diagonal one.

The extremes J = empty (ordinary KL basis on S_n) and J = S (^JW = {e}, rank-one module) are inside the construction; the induced bar-duality matrix R has diagonal one in all cases. See the Statement and the numbered verification steps.

The uniqueness step takes the Bruhat-maximal element of a hypothetical nonzero support, the endpoint of a finite lower ideal; no limiting process occurs. See the Statement and the numbered verification steps.
Explicitly choice-free: step 2.1 runs a finite induction over the finite poset (^JW, <=) and states that no choice principle is used.

boundaries.reason: The theorem asserts existence and uniqueness with characterizing properties (i)-(ii); there is no biconditional between separate conditions.
No converse is asserted beyond uniqueness, which is proved directly in step 4.1 for an arbitrary bar-fixed element of the prescribed support.

reader_repair.description: R bar(R)=I and its inverse identity explicitly distinguished; coefficient induction increases length gap.

risk_review.notes: On each finite lower ideal bar squared gives R bar(R)=I; unitriangular invertibility gives the reversed product needed by induction. Increasing the length gap constructs coefficients above x first. Anti-invariance makes the constant Laurent coefficient zero and its positive part solves c-bar(c)=a. Maximal-support uniqueness and finite unitriangular inversion prove both bases. The trivial/full parabolic and rank-zero generator cases reduce to the same calculation, without AC or unstated positivity.

citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Work in category
$\mathcal O$ with the conventions of the preceding definitions. For a weight
$\lambda$ write $\chi_\lambda$ for the generalized central character obtained
from $\lambda$, so that $\chi_\lambda=\chi_\mu$ if and only if
$\mu\in W\mathbin\cdot\lambda$
([[cor-central-characters-are-dot-weyl-orbits]]), and let
$\mathcal O=\bigoplus_\chi\mathcal O_\chi$ be the central-character
decomposition of [[thm-category-o-decomposes-by-generalized-central-character]]
with inclusions $\operatorname{incl}_\chi$ and exact projections
$\operatorname{pr}_\chi$, so that
$\operatorname{pr}_\chi\circ\operatorname{incl}_\chi=\operatorname{id}$.

For a finite-dimensional $\mathfrak h$-semisimple $\mathfrak g$-module $E$
([[def-weight-and-weight-space-of-a-lie-algebra-representation]]) and two
generalized central characters $\chi,\chi'$, set
$$T_{\chi,E,\chi'}:=\operatorname{pr}_{\chi'}\circ(E\otimes-)\circ\operatorname{incl}_\chi\colon\mathcal O_\chi\longrightarrow\mathcal O_{\chi'}.$$
This is well defined because $E\otimes-$ is an exact endofunctor of
$\mathcal O$
([[prop-tensoring-with-a-finite-dimensional-module-preserves-category-o]])
and the projections and inclusions are exact.

For weights $\lambda,\mu$ with $\mu-\lambda$ integral
([[def-dot-action-facets-and-single-wall-translation-data]]), let $\nu$ be the
unique dominant weight in the linear Weyl orbit $W(\mu-\lambda)$, which exists
and is unique by [[lem-finite-weyl-closed-chambers-and-stabilizers]] and is
integral; let $L(\nu)$ be the finite-dimensional simple module of highest
weight $\nu$
([[thm-finite-dimensional-simple-modules-are-classified-by-dominant-highest-weights]]).
Define
$$T_\lambda^\mu:=T_{\chi_\lambda,L(\nu),\chi_\mu}\colon\mathcal O_{\chi_\lambda}\longrightarrow\mathcal O_{\chi_\mu},\qquad T_\mu^\lambda:=T_{\chi_\mu,L(\nu)^*,\chi_\lambda}\colon\mathcal O_{\chi_\mu}\longrightarrow\mathcal O_{\chi_\lambda},$$
where $L(\nu)^*$ is the ordinary linear dual, a finite-dimensional
$\mathfrak h$-semisimple simple module isomorphic to $L(-w_0\nu)$ by
[[prop-highest-weight-of-the-dual-representation]].

The labels $\lambda$ and $\mu$ denote actual weights and not $\rho$-shifted
parameters. The central-character subcategories used here are those of the
published decomposition; a central-character summand can contain several
linkage blocks of
[[thm-central-character-summands-split-into-linkage-blocks]], while for an
indecomposable central-character summand the present functors are translation
between that summand and its target.

Fix a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$, a Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$, and a positive Borel $\mathfrak b=\mathfrak h\oplus\mathfrak n^+$. Write $Q^+=\sum_i\mathbb Z_{\geq0}\alpha_i$, $\mu\leq\lambda$ when $\lambda-\mu\in Q^+$, and $w\cdot\lambda=w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho$.

The category is the categorical direct sum $\mathcal O=\bigoplus_\chi\mathcal O_\chi$: objects have finite support in the index $\chi$, morphisms between distinct components vanish, and the canonical component projections are exact.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra with Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$, a chosen positive-root system and corresponding Borel, Weyl group $W$, and half-sum $\rho$ of positive roots. Let $\chi_\lambda$ and $\chi_\mu$ be the central characters obtained from highest weights $\lambda,\mu\in\mathfrak h^*$ for this Borel. Then

$$\chi_\lambda=\chi_\mu \quad \text{if and only if} \quad \mu\in W\cdot \lambda,$$

where $W\cdot \lambda:=\{w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho : w\in W\}$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). For every
finite-dimensional $\mathfrak h$-semisimple $\mathfrak g$-module $E$ the
translation functor $T_{\chi,E,\chi'}$
([[def-translation-functor-between-o-blocks]]) is exact, and
$T_{\chi',E^*,\chi}$ is both a left and a right adjoint of
$T_{\chi,E,\chi'}$; in particular both functors send projectives to
projectives and injectives to injectives. Consequently, in the setting of
[[def-translation-functor-between-o-blocks]], $T_\mu^\lambda$ is both a left
and a right adjoint of $T_\lambda^\mu$, and the two functors are exact.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\lambda$ be an
integral dot-antidominant dot-regular weight and let $\mu$ be an integral
dot-antidominant weight such that the facet $F_\mu$ lies in the closure of the
chamber $F_\lambda$, i.e.
$\langle\mu+\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle=0$ for the positive roots
$\alpha\in\Phi_J^+$ of the parabolic subsystem $\Phi_J$ of
$J=J(\mu)$ defined in
[[def-singular-integral-category-o-block-and-stabilizer]], and
$\langle\mu+\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle$ has the same sign as
$\langle\lambda+\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle$ for every remaining positive root
([[def-dot-action-facets-and-single-wall-translation-data]]). Let $\nu$ be the
unique dominant weight of the linear orbit $W(\mu-\lambda)$
([[lem-finite-weyl-closed-chambers-and-stabilizers]]) and let
$E=L(\nu)$
([[thm-finite-dimensional-simple-modules-are-classified-by-dominant-highest-weights]]).
Then for all $w,w'\in W$ and every weight $\gamma$ of $E$: if
$w'\cdot\mu=w\cdot\lambda+\gamma$, then $w'\cdot\mu=w\cdot\mu$ and
$\gamma=w(\mu-\lambda)$.

Consequently, for every $w$ the tensor $E\otimes\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)$ has
exactly one Verma factor whose central character is that of $\mu$, namely
$\Delta(w\cdot\mu)$, and its multiplicity in the Verma flag computed by
[[lem-tensoring-with-a-finite-dimensional-module-preserves-verma-flags]] is
one.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $E$ be a
finite-dimensional $\mathfrak h$-semisimple $\mathfrak g$-module with weight
multiplicities $\dim E_\eta$
([[def-weight-and-weight-space-of-a-lie-algebra-representation]]). For every
weight $\mu$, the object $E\otimes\Delta(\mu)$ has a finite Verma flag
([[def-verma-flag-and-its-multiplicities]]) whose factors are $\Delta(\mu+\eta)$,
the factor $\Delta(\mu+\eta)$ occurring $\dim E_\eta$ times; the factors can be
ordered so that a real-linear height $\ell$ with $\ell(\alpha_i)=1$ is nonincreasing.

Consequently, if $X\in\mathcal O$ has a finite Verma flag with multiplicities
$(X:\Delta(\nu))$, then $E\otimes X$ has a finite Verma flag and
$$(E\otimes X:\Delta(\mu))=\sum_\eta\dim E_\eta\,(X:\Delta(\mu-\eta)).$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), inherited from the
published block theory. Work in category $\mathcal O$ of a finite-dimensional
complex semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ with Cartan $\mathfrak h$,
positive system $\Phi^+$, simple roots $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_r$, Weyl group
$W$, Weyl vector $\rho$ and dot action $w\cdot\lambda=w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho$, as
in [[def-bgg-category-o]] and
[[def-dot-action-facets-and-single-wall-translation-data]].

**(1) Dot-antidominant integral weights.** A weight $\mu$ is **dot-antidominant**
if $\langle\mu+\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle\le0$ for every $\alpha\in\Phi^+$, and
**integral** if $\langle\mu,\alpha_i^\vee\rangle\in\mathbb Z$ for all $i$
([[def-integral-weyl-group-of-a-weight]],
[[def-integral-dominant-and-strictly-dominant-weights]]).

**(2) The dot stabilizer.** Fix such a weight $\mu$ and put
$$J=J(\mu):=\{i:\langle\mu+\rho,\alpha_i^\vee\rangle=0\},\qquad W_\mu:=W_J=\langle s_i:i\in J\rangle.$$
Then the dot stabilizer $\{v\in W:v\cdot\mu=\mu\}$ equals $W_J$. Indeed, for
$i\in J$ the reflection $s_i$ fixes $\mu+\rho$, so $W_J$ lies in the
stabilizer; conversely the stabilizer of an integral dot-antidominant weight
is generated by the reflections it contains and is a standard parabolic
([[lem-finite-weyl-closed-chambers-and-stabilizers]], applied to the dominant
vector $-\mu-\rho$), and by
[[def-cg-parabolic-quotient-and-two-sided-minima]] a standard parabolic
subgroup is $W_I$ for the set $I$ of simple reflections it contains, which is
exactly $J$. In particular $w'\cdot\mu=w\cdot\mu$ if and only if
$w^{-1}w'\in W_J$, that is, $w'\in wW_J$.

**(3) The singular integral block.** The **singular integral block**
$\mathcal O_\mu$ is the block of
[[thm-central-character-summands-split-into-linkage-blocks]] of the central
character $\chi_\mu$ of $\mu$; by
[[cor-central-characters-are-dot-weyl-orbits]] two central characters agree
exactly when the highest weights lie in one dot orbit, and by
[[thm-category-o-decomposes-by-generalized-central-character]] the block is a
summand of $\mathcal O$. Its simple objects $L(w\cdot\mu)$, standard objects
$\Delta(w\cdot\mu)=M(w\cdot\mu)$, costandard objects $\nabla(w\cdot\mu)$ and
projective covers $P(w\cdot\mu)$ are indexed by $w\in W$
([[def-standard-and-costandard-objects-in-category-o]],
[[def-verma-module]]); by (2) the label $w\cdot\mu$ depends only on the coset
$wW_J$, so the labels can be normalized by the minimal right coset
representatives

$$W^J=\{w\in W:\ell(ws)>\ell(w)\ \text{for all }s\in J\},$$

which are exactly the elements of minimal length in the cosets $wW_J$
([[thm-hh-parabolic-minimal-representatives-and-length-additivity]] (3));
inversion carries $W^J$ onto the minimal left coset representatives ${}^JW$,
and the two families are the label sets of the parabolic Hecke modules of
[[def-parabolic-hecke-module-and-antispherical-standard-basis]].

**(4) Highest-weight structure and multiplicities.** The block is a
highest-weight category: it has enough projectives
([[thm-category-o-has-enough-projectives]]), projective covers have finite
Verma flags ([[thm-projectives-in-category-o-have-verma-flags]]), the standard
classes and simple classes are bases of the Grothendieck group
([[def-grothendieck-group-and-character-of-category-o]],
[[prop-the-grothendieck-group-of-o-has-simple-and-standard-bases]]), and it
satisfies BGG reciprocity
$$(P(w\cdot\mu):\Delta(y\cdot\mu))=[M(y\cdot\mu):L(w\cdot\mu)]$$
([[thm-bgg-reciprocity]], [[def-verma-flag-and-its-multiplicities]]). The
multiplicity matrix is unitriangular for the refinement of the dominance order
on the dot orbit: $(P(w\cdot\mu):\Delta(w\cdot\mu))=1$, and
$(P(w\cdot\mu):\Delta(y\cdot\mu))\neq0$ only if $y\cdot\mu\ge w\cdot\mu$
([[cor-projective-standard-labels-lie-above-the-head]]); the ordinary
standard/costandard Hom and $\mathrm{Ext}^1$ vanishing used on this page is
[[lem-standard-costandard-hom-and-ext-vanishing]].

**(5) Regular versus singular.** The block is **regular** when $J=\varnothing$
(the weight lies on no wall) and **singular** when $J\neq\varnothing$; the
singular translation statements of this page use this notation, and
$J=\varnothing$ recovers the regular case. The genuine regular-parabolic
multiplicity statements below have their own separate explicit dominant
regular base and are not consequences of the notation here.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Fix a finite-dimensional
complex semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$, a Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$,
and a positive Borel $\mathfrak b=\mathfrak h\oplus\mathfrak n^+$, with the
chosen positive system $\Phi^+$ and Weyl vector $\rho$ of
[[def-weyl-vector-rho-for-a-chosen-positive-system]] and Weyl group $W$ acting
by the root reflections
$s_\alpha(\lambda)=\lambda-\lambda(\alpha^\vee)\alpha$ of
[[def-root-reflections-and-the-weyl-group-action]]. Write the dot action as
$w\mathbin\cdot\lambda=w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho$ and write
$\langle\zeta,\alpha^\vee\rangle$ for the pairing with the coroot
([[thm-the-root-set-is-a-reduced-crystallographic-root-system]]).

Put $R=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\Phi\subseteq\mathfrak h^*$. For a weight
$\lambda\in R$, the **dot-Weyl facet** of $\lambda$ is
the set of weights
$$F_\lambda=\{\zeta\in R:\ \operatorname{sgn}\langle\zeta+\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle=\operatorname{sgn}\langle\lambda+\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle\ \text{for every root }\alpha\in\Phi\},$$
where $\operatorname{sgn}$ takes the values positive, zero and negative. Its
**upper closure** is
$$F_\lambda^+=\{\zeta\in R:\ \langle\zeta+\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle\ \text{is positive, zero or nonpositive according as}\ \langle\lambda+\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle\ \text{is positive, zero or negative, for every }\alpha\in\Phi^+\}.$$
The upper-closure test uses only positive roots: imposing it also on their
negatives would incorrectly exclude wall points from the upper closure of
the antidominant chamber. Thus $F_\lambda\subseteq F_\lambda^+$, the facets refine the closures of the
open Weyl chambers, and $F_\lambda$ depends only on the wall-sign pattern of
$\lambda+\rho$.

Two special positions are used throughout. A weight $\lambda$ is **dot-regular**
when $\langle\lambda+\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle\neq0$ for every root $\alpha$, so
that $F_\lambda$ is an open chamber; it is **dot-antidominant** when
$\langle\lambda+\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle\le0$ for every positive root $\alpha$.
Integrality of weights is the notion of
[[def-integral-dominant-and-strictly-dominant-weights]].

A **single-wall translation datum** is a triple $(\lambda,\mu,\alpha)$
consisting of integral dot-antidominant weights $\lambda,\mu$ and a positive
root $\alpha$ such that:

1. $\lambda$ is dot-regular, so $F_\lambda$ is an open chamber;
2. $\mu+\rho$ lies in the closure of the chamber of $\lambda+\rho$: one has
   $\langle\mu+\rho,\alpha^\vee\rangle=0$, and
   $\langle\mu+\rho,\beta^\vee\rangle$ has the same sign as
   $\langle\lambda+\rho,\beta^\vee\rangle$ for every root $\beta$ different
   from $\alpha$ and from its multiples;
3. the dot stabilizer $S_\mu:=\{w\in W:w\mathbin\cdot\mu=\mu\}$ is exactly $\{1,s_\alpha\}$.

Equivalently, $F_\mu$ is a codimension-one facet in the closure of the open
antidominant chamber $F_\lambda$, with $S_\mu=\{1,s_\alpha\}$.
This dot stabilizer and the integral-reflection group $W_\mu$ of
[[def-integral-weyl-group-of-a-weight]] are defined by different conditions:
since $\mu$ is integral, all simple reflections belong to $W_\mu$, so
$W_\mu=W$, whereas $S_\mu=\{1,s_\alpha\}$. The groups coincide in rank one
and differ when the rank is greater than one. In
this datum the **translating weight** $\nu$ is the unique dominant weight of
the linear Weyl orbit $W(\mu-\lambda)$; it exists and is unique by
[[lem-finite-weyl-closed-chambers-and-stabilizers]], and it is integral because
$\mu-\lambda$ is integral and $W$ preserves the weight lattice. The **wall
reflection** is $s:=s_\alpha$.

The basic example is $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ with the datum
$(\lambda,\mu)=(-2,-1)$: here $\rho=1$, $\mu=-\rho$,
$\lambda+\rho=-1$ spans the open negative chamber, $\mu+\rho=0$ is the single
wall, and the dot-stabilizer of $\mu$ is $\{1,s\}$. The pair $(0,-1)$ uses the dominant regular representative rather than the
antidominant representative required here. It defines the same translation
functors: $0$ and $-2$ have the same central character, and both weight
differences have dominant representative $1$ with translating module
$L(1)$, which is self-dual. These functors are defined in
the next definition on this page.

Assume the Axiom of Choice.

Fix a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$, a Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$, and a positive Borel $\mathfrak b=\mathfrak h\oplus\mathfrak n^+$. Write $Q^+=\sum_i\mathbb Z_{\geq0}\alpha_i$, $\mu\leq\lambda$ when $\lambda-\mu\in Q^+$, and $w\cdot\lambda=w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho$.

Restricted Chevalley duality is an exact contravariant equivalence $D:\mathcal O\to\mathcal O^{\mathrm{op}}$, with a natural isomorphism $D^2\cong\operatorname{id}$. It preserves each weight-space dimension, the formal character, and every simple composition multiplicity.

Fix a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$, a Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$, and a positive Borel $\mathfrak b=\mathfrak h\oplus\mathfrak n^+$. Write $Q^+=\sum_i\mathbb Z_{\geq0}\alpha_i$, $\mu\leq\lambda$ when $\lambda-\mu\in Q^+$, and $w\cdot\lambda=w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho$.

For $\lambda\in\mathfrak h^*$, define the **standard** and **costandard** weight modules by

$$\Delta(\lambda)=M(\lambda),\qquad\nabla(\lambda)=D(M(\lambda)).$$

The Verma module is defined in [[def-verma-module]], and its restricted dual is defined in [[def-restricted-dual-of-a-weight-module]]. Under the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), [[prop-restricted-duality-is-an-exact-involution-on-category-o]] places $\nabla(\lambda)$ in $\mathcal O$, so both displayed modules are objects of that category. These symbols impose no projectivity or highest-weight-category axiom.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\nu$ be a dominant
integral weight
([[def-integral-dominant-and-strictly-dominant-weights]]) and let $\gamma$ be
a weight of the finite-dimensional simple module $L(\nu)$
([[thm-finite-dimensional-simple-modules-are-classified-by-dominant-highest-weights]]).
Then, in the $W$-invariant positive definite form on the real span $E$ of the
roots ([[prop-the-roots-form-a-reduced-crystallographic-euclidean-root-system]]),
$$\lvert\gamma\rvert\le\lvert\nu\rvert,$$
with equality if and only if $\gamma$ lies in the Weyl orbit $W\nu$; moreover
every weight in $W\nu$ occurs in $L(\nu)$ with multiplicity one.

The proper submodule $J(\lambda)$ which is the sum of all proper submodules is
the unique maximal submodule of $M(\lambda)$.  The quotient
$L(\lambda):=M(\lambda)/J(\lambda)$ is simple and is its unique simple
quotient.

Assume the Axiom of Choice.

For weights $\lambda,\mu$, a nonzero homomorphism $M(\mu)\to M(\lambda)$ exists if and only if $\mu\uparrow\lambda$.
Every nonzero $\mathfrak g$-homomorphism $M(\mu)\to M(\lambda)$ is injective.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). For all weights
$\lambda$ and $\mu$,
$$(P(\lambda):\Delta(\mu))=[\Delta(\mu):L(\lambda)]=[M(\mu):L(\lambda)],$$
where $P(\lambda)$ is the projective cover of $L(\lambda)$, the left-hand
multiplicity is the Verma-flag multiplicity of
[[thm-projectives-in-category-o-have-verma-flags]], and the right-hand
multiplicity is the simple composition multiplicity of the Verma module
$M(\mu)$ ([[def-standard-and-costandard-objects-in-category-o]]).

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Work in category
$\mathcal O$ with the conventions of [[def-bgg-category-o]], and write
$\Delta(\mu)=M(\mu)$ for the standard objects of
[[def-standard-and-costandard-objects-in-category-o]], i.e. the Verma modules
of [[def-verma-module]].

A **finite Verma flag** of an object $X$ of $\mathcal O$ — also called a
**standard flag** or a **$\Delta$-flag** — is a finite increasing sequence of
subobjects
$$0=X_0\subseteq X_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq X_n=X$$
such that each quotient $X_i/X_{i-1}$ is isomorphic to a Verma module
$\Delta(\mu_i)=M(\mu_i)$, for $i=1,\dots,n$. An object admitting such a flag is
called **Verma-filtered**. Since the flag is exhausted by its factors, its
class in the Grothendieck group
$K_0(\mathcal O)$ of [[def-grothendieck-group-and-character-of-category-o]]
is
$$[X]=\sum_{i=1}^n[\Delta(\mu_i)].$$

For a Verma-filtered object $X$ and a weight $\mu$, the **multiplicity**
$(X:\Delta(\mu))$ is the number of indices $i$ with $\mu_i=\mu$ in a Verma
flag of $X$. This number is independent of the chosen flag by
[[lem-verma-flag-multiplicities-are-independent-of-the-flag]], so the notation
$(X:\Delta(\mu))$ is well-defined for Verma-filtered $X$.

The zero object has the empty flag, and every multiplicity of the zero object
is zero; a nonzero Verma-filtered object has at least one factor. A one-step
flag of $X$ is exactly an isomorphism $X\cong\Delta(\mu)$ for a single weight
$\mu$, so the objects with a one-step flag are the Verma modules themselves.
The flag is a chain of subobjects of $X$ in the module category; it is not
required to split, and later examples show that it need not.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Every projective object
of $\mathcal O$ has a finite Verma flag
([[def-verma-flag-and-its-multiplicities]]).

More precisely, each projective cover $P(\mu)$ produced by
[[thm-category-o-has-enough-projectives]] is a direct summand of the
projective object $\operatorname{pr}_C(E\otimes M(\lambda))$ of
[[lem-finite-dimensional-tensors-reach-every-block-simple]], which is a
direct summand of $E\otimes M(\lambda)$; a general projective object has
finite length, hence is a finite direct sum of indecomposable projectives,
each of which is a projective cover of its simple head.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). For all weights $\mu$
and $
u$ one has
$$\dim_{\mathbb C}\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O}(\Delta(\mu),
abla(
u))=1\ 	ext{if }\mu=
u,\qquad\dim_{\mathbb C}\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O}(\Delta(\mu),
abla(
u))=0\ 	ext{if }\mu
e
u,$$
and
$$\operatorname{Ext}^1_{\mathcal O}(\Delta(\mu),
abla(
u))=0 .$$
Here $\Delta(
u)=M(
u)$ and $
abla(
u)=D(M(
u))$ are the standard and
costandard objects of
[[def-standard-and-costandard-objects-in-category-o]], and
$\operatorname{Ext}^1$ is the derived Ext over the abelian category
$\mathcal O$, identified with classes of extensions by the Yoneda theorem.

Fix a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$, a Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$, and a positive Borel $\mathfrak b=\mathfrak h\oplus\mathfrak n^+$. Write $Q^+=\sum_i\mathbb Z_{\geq0}\alpha_i$, $\mu\leq\lambda$ when $\lambda-\mu\in Q^+$, and $w\cdot\lambda=w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho$.

The simple objects of $\mathcal O$ are exactly the modules $L(\lambda)$, $\lambda\in\mathfrak h^*$, and $L(\lambda)\cong L(\mu)$ if and only if $\lambda=\mu$. Simplicity here excludes zero.

Let $\mathcal A$ be an abelian category in which every object has finite
length, and define an object to be **indecomposable** when it is nonzero and
every decomposition $X\cong Y\oplus Z$ has $Y=0$ or $Z=0$. Then:

1. every object of $\mathcal A$ is a finite direct sum of indecomposable
   objects;
2. the endomorphism ring of an indecomposable object is local, and for an
   endomorphism $f$ of an indecomposable object either $f$ is an isomorphism
   or $f$ is nilpotent;
3. the decomposition is unique up to isomorphism and permutation of the
   summands;
4. an indecomposable projective object $P$ of $\mathcal A$ has a unique
   maximal proper subobject $J(P)$, its quotient $P/J(P)$ is simple, and $P$
   is a projective cover of $P/J(P)$
   ([[def-projective-object]], [[def-essential-epimorphism-and-projective-cover]];
   projectivity here is relative to $\mathcal A$. In a full subcategory closed
   under submodules, essentiality is the superfluous-kernel condition of the
   cited module definition; projectivity in the ambient module category is
   not asserted).

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). If a projective object
$P$ of $\mathcal O$ admits an epimorphism $P\twoheadrightarrow L$ onto a
simple object $L$, then some indecomposable direct summand of $P$ maps onto
$L$, and that summand is a projective cover of $L$ (an essential epimorphism
with projective source, [[def-essential-epimorphism-and-projective-cover]]).
Any two projective covers of $L$ are isomorphic, although not canonically so,
and the endomorphism ring of a projective cover is local. In particular, for
every simple $L$ there is at most one isomorphism class of indecomposable
projectives with head $L$; when such a cover exists it is written $P(L)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Every simple object
$L(\mu)$ of $\mathcal O$ admits a projective cover
$P(\mu)\twoheadrightarrow L(\mu)$
([[def-essential-epimorphism-and-projective-cover]]), which may be chosen
inside the linkage class of $\mu$; the cover is unique up to isomorphism and
indecomposable. Consequently $\mathcal O$ has enough projectives: every object
of $\mathcal O$ is a quotient of a finite direct sum of such projective
covers, because objects of $\mathcal O$ have finite length and each composition
factor is a quotient of its projective cover.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\zeta\in\mathfrak h^*$ be a **dominant integral weight**, that is,
$\langle\zeta,\alpha_i^\vee\rangle\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$ for every simple root
$\alpha_i$ (equivalently, when $\zeta$ lies in the real span of the roots,
$\langle\zeta,\alpha^\vee\rangle\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$ for every positive root
$\alpha$). Then
$$\zeta-w\zeta\in Q^+\qquad\text{for every }w\in W,$$
where $W$ is the Weyl group of
[[def-root-reflections-and-the-weyl-group-action]] and $Q^+$ is the cone of
[[def-partial-order-on-weights]]. In particular $\zeta$ is the maximum of its
Weyl orbit for the order $\mu\le\nu$ defined by $\nu-\mu\in Q^+$, and if
$w\zeta\ge\zeta$ then $w\zeta=\zeta$.

Consequently, if $\lambda$ is a weight with $\lambda+\rho$ dominant integral
($\rho$ the Weyl vector of [[def-weyl-vector-rho-for-a-chosen-positive-system]]),
then $\lambda-w\mathbin\cdot\lambda\in Q^+$ for every $w\in W$, and $\lambda$
is the maximum of its linkage class $W_\lambda\mathbin\cdot\lambda$ of
[[def-integral-weyl-group-of-a-weight]]; here
$W_\lambda=W$ because every simple reflection pairs integrally with
$\lambda+\rho$.

Integrality is used with its full strength: for a dominant $\zeta$ that is not
integral the conclusion $\zeta-w\zeta\in Q^+$ fails for reflections pairing
non-integrally with $\zeta$, and only the reflections integral at $\zeta$ can
be used.

The weights of $M(\lambda)$ are exactly $\lambda-\beta$ for
$\beta\in Q^+$; every weight space is finite dimensional, and
$M(\lambda)_\lambda=\mathbb Cv_\lambda$.

For the simple reflections of a finite reduced crystallographic root system, word length equals inversion length: $\ell(w)=|\operatorname{Inv}(w)|$. If a root reflection $t$ satisfies $\ell(tw)<\ell(w)$, every reduced word for $w$ loses exactly one letter to give $tw$. Every nonreduced word admits deletion of two letters without changing its group element.

More precisely, for $\beta\in\Phi^+$, $\ell(s_\beta w)<\ell(w)$ if and only if $w^{-1}\beta<0$. In this case one letter can be deleted from any word for $w$ to give $s_\beta w$, although the resulting word need not be reduced. Also $\ell(ws_i)=\ell(w)\pm1$, with the minus sign exactly when $w\alpha_i<0$. These are assertions for the geometric reflection group, without an assumed Coxeter presentation or exchange axiom.

derivations.claim: **Standards (first clause of (1)).** By [F3], the tensor $E\otimes\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)$ has a finite Verma flag by [F4] in which the unique factor with central character $\chi_\mu$ is $\Delta(w\cdot\mu)$, once. The exact projection $\operatorname{pr}_{\chi_\mu}$ applied to this flag kills every factor whose central character differs from $\chi_\mu$ and carries the remaining $\Delta(w\cdot\mu)$ isomorphically, so $T\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)\cong\Delta(w\cdot\mu)$ for every $w$.

**The big projective (3).** By [F9], $M(-\rho)=L(-\rho)$. Its dot orbit is a singleton, so BGG reciprocity [F7] gives a one-factor Verma flag for $P(-\rho)$, proving $P(-\rho)=L(-\rho)$. Simple-preserving duality makes it injective too. Put $E_0=L(w_0\mu_\bullet)$ and $S=T_{-\rho}^{\mu}$, whose adjoint is $S'=T_{\mu}^{-\rho}$; the ordinary dual $E_0^*$ has highest weight $-\mu_\bullet$. By [F2], $\Xi_\mu=SL(-\rho)$ is projective and injective. Tensoring $M(-\rho)$ with $E_0$ and projecting retains exactly the factors $\Delta(-\rho+\gamma)$ with $\gamma\in W\mu_\bullet$, each once by [F4], [F8]. These are precisely the distinct standards $\Delta(y\cdot\mu)$. Likewise, since $L(\mu)=M(\mu)$ by [F9], tensoring it with $E_0^*$ and projecting to $\chi_{-\rho}$ retains only $\Delta(-\rho)$, once, from the extremal weight $-\mu_\bullet$. Thus $S'L(\mu)=L(-\rho)$, and adjunction gives $\dim\operatorname{Hom}(\Xi_\mu,L(\mu))=1$. The resulting epimorphism splits off the projective cover $P(\mu)$: lift it through the cover, use essentiality to make the lift surjective, and split by projectivity. For every $y$, there is an injection $M(\mu)\hookrightarrow M(y\cdot\mu)$. Indeed induct on a reduced expression $y=s_i v$: [F10] gives $v^{-1}\alpha_i>0$, so $\langle v(\mu_\bullet),\alpha_i^\vee\rangle\le0$. If it is zero the weights coincide; otherwise the positive integral pairing at $s_i v\cdot\mu$ supplies the one-step strong linkage and the injection $M(v\cdot\mu)\hookrightarrow M(s_i v\cdot\mu)$ by [F7]. Compose these injections. BGG then gives $(P(\mu):\Delta(y\cdot\mu))\ge1$ for every distinct label. The direct-summand complement of $P(\mu)$ in $\Xi_\mu$ is projective and has a Verma flag by [F7]. Additivity and the already computed one-per-label flag of $\Xi_\mu$ force every flag multiplicity of the complement to vanish, so the complement is zero. Hence $\Xi_\mu=P(\mu)$ and all the displayed standard and composition multiplicities are one.

**Nonminimal vanishing (second half of (2)).** Suppose $w\notin W^J$; then there is a simple $s\in J$ with $\ell(ws)<\ell(w)$, equivalently $w\alpha_s<0$ by [F10]. Then $w\cdot\lambda-ws\cdot\lambda=w(\lambda-s\cdot\lambda)=\langle\lambda_\bullet,\alpha_s^\vee\rangle\,w\alpha_s$ with $\langle\lambda_\bullet,\alpha_s^\vee\rangle<0$ and $w\alpha_s<0$, so $w\cdot\lambda-ws\cdot\lambda\in Q^+\setminus\{0\}$: $ws\cdot\lambda$ is strictly below $w\cdot\lambda$. Put $\beta=-w\alpha_s\in\Phi^+$; then $s_\beta w=ws$ and $\langle w\lambda_\bullet,\beta^\vee\rangle=-\langle\lambda_\bullet,\alpha_s^\vee\rangle\in\mathbb Z_{>0}$. This is a one-step strong linkage, so [F7] gives a nonzero (hence injective) map $\Delta(ws\cdot\lambda)\to\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)$ by [F7]. Applying the exact functor $T$ and step 1.1 gives a map $\Delta(ws\cdot\mu)\to\Delta(w\cdot\mu)$; now $ws\cdot\mu=w\cdot(s\cdot\mu)=w\cdot\mu$ because $s\in J$ fixes $\mu$ [F5], so this is an injective endomorphism of the finite-length module $\Delta(w\cdot\mu)$, hence an isomorphism. If $N$ is the cokernel of $\Delta(ws\cdot\lambda)\to\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)$, exactness of $T$ gives $TN=0$; since $L(w\cdot\lambda)$ is a quotient of $N$ (the kernel of $\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)\twoheadrightarrow L(w\cdot\lambda)$ contains $\Delta(ws\cdot\lambda)$ because the latter has no composition factor $L(w\cdot\lambda)$, its weights being strictly below), $TL(w\cdot\lambda)=0$.

**Costandards (second clause of (1)).** The evaluation pairing gives $D(E\otimes M)\cong D(E)\otimes D(M)$ naturally, and $D(E)\cong E$ for the finite-dimensional simple $E$ by [F6]. Hence $E\otimes
abla(w\cdot\lambda)=E\otimes D\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)\cong D(E\otimes\Delta(w\cdot\lambda))$. Since $D$ preserves central-character blocks and is exact, it commutes with the inclusion and projection defining the translation functor, so $T
abla(w\cdot\lambda)=\operatorname{pr}_{\chi_\mu}(E\otimes
abla(w\cdot\lambda))\cong D(\operatorname{pr}_{\chi_\mu}(E\otimes\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)))\cong D\Delta(w\cdot\mu)=
abla(w\cdot\mu)$ by step 1.1.

**A translated simple is simple or zero.** For every $x\in W$, apply exact $T$ to $\Delta(x\cdot\lambda)\twoheadrightarrow L(x\cdot\lambda)\hookrightarrow\nabla(x\cdot\lambda)$. Steps 1.1 and 2.2 give a surjection $\Delta(x\cdot\mu)\twoheadrightarrow TL(x\cdot\lambda)$ followed by an injection into $\nabla(x\cdot\mu)$. If the intermediate object is nonzero, the composite is nonzero; the one-dimensional standard-costandard Hom of [F7] makes its image the canonical simple $L(x\cdot\mu)$. The injection identifies the intermediate object with that image. Thus $TL(x\cdot\lambda)$ is either zero or $L(x\cdot\mu)$, without any unstated Bruhat support assertion.

**Minimal survival.** Let $w\in W^J$ and translate a composition series of $\Delta(w\cdot\lambda)$. Its image is $\Delta(w\cdot\mu)$, whose head $L(w\cdot\mu)$ occurs as a composition factor. By step 3.1 that factor is the image of some $L(x\cdot\lambda)$ with $x\cdot\mu=w\cdot\mu$. Step 2.1 kills every nonminimal $x$, and [F5] says that the coset $wW_J$ has exactly one minimal representative, namely $w$. Thus $TL(w\cdot\lambda)$ is nonzero and equals $L(w\cdot\mu)$ by step 3.1. Together with step 2.1 this proves (2).
Part (1) is steps 1.1 and 2.2; part (2) is steps 2.1 and 3.1 together with the simplicity statement of step 4.1; part (3) is step 1.2.

boundaries.evidence: W^J = W when J = empty, so the killing case of (2) is empty and every simple survives, consistent with the regular case; no other empty family occurs. See the Statement and the numbered verification steps.
TL(w.lambda) = 0 for w not in W^J is the central zero statement, proved in step 2.1 through an injective endomorphism of Delta(w.mu); the cokernel object N there satisfies TN = 0.
F9 covers singular antidominant simplicity including -rho; step 1.2 computes the two exact projected tensor flags and the projective complement, giving multiplicity one for every distinct label.

J=empty and J=S are included; F9 proves M(-rho)=L(-rho) without the strict-antidominant hypothesis; the simple/coset and big-projective calculations also apply in rank zero. See step 1.2 and steps 3.1–4.1.

lambda and mu are dot-antidominant orbit endpoints with F_mu in the closure of F_lambda; the labels -rho and the coset minima W^J are the extremal label sets used. See the Statement and the numbered verification steps.

The Axiom of Choice is declared and inherited from the translation-functor and duality suppliers; the representative nu of W(mu-lambda) is the unique dominant one, hence canonical. See the Statement and the numbered verification steps.
The dichotomy (2), forward: TL(w.lambda) not equal to 0 implies w in W^J; the contrapositive (nonminimal vanishing) is step 2.1.
Steps 3.1 and 4.1 first prove the simple-or-zero sandwich, then the existence of a surviving factor and the unique minimal representative in its coset.

reader_repair.description: F9 proves singular antidominant simplicity; F10 supplies root signs; corrected duals, big projective and sandwich/coset survival; actual upper closure.

risk_review.notes: Exact central projection retains the single facet-exclusion standard. Chevalley D(E), distinct from the ordinary adjoint dual E*, commutes with tensor translation and yields costandards. For nonminimal w the reflection beta=-w alpha_s gives a positive integral one-step linkage, and exact translation makes the embedding an endomorphism isomorphism. The standard/costandard sandwich proves simple-or-zero before unique-minimal-coset survival. Orbit lower bounds and Verma upper bounds prove singular antidominant simplicity. Translation of L(-rho) has one flag section per distinct label; the correct E0 dual and adjunction split off P(mu), and root-reflection embeddings force the projective complement to have zero flag. Positive signs remain strict in upper closure. J=empty/S, mu=-rho, and the sl2 wall cases match all three conclusions; AC is inherited.

citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), inherited from the
published category-$\mathcal O$ theory. Let
$\mathfrak p=\mathfrak p_J=\mathfrak l_J\oplus\mathfrak u_J$ be the standard
parabolic of
[[def-standard-parabolic-and-levi-subalgebras-from-simple-roots]], with
reductive parabolic Levi $\mathfrak l_J$, nilradical $\mathfrak u_J$ and Weyl
group $W_J$; the ambient category is $\mathcal O$ of [[def-bgg-category-o]]
with standard objects the Verma modules [[def-verma-module]].

**(1) Dominance for the Levi.** A weight $\lambda$ is **$\mathfrak p$-dominant**
if $\langle\lambda,\alpha^\vee\rangle\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$ for all
$\alpha\in\Phi_J^+$ (this is dominance for the Levi root system; in particular
$\lambda$ is integral for $\Phi_J$; see
[[def-integral-dominant-and-strictly-dominant-weights]] for the ambient
notion).

**(2) Generalized Verma modules.** For a $\mathfrak p$-dominant $\lambda$ let
$E(\lambda)$ be the finite-dimensional simple $\mathfrak p$-module obtained
from the finite-dimensional simple $\mathfrak l_J$-module of highest weight
$\lambda$
([[thm-finite-dimensional-simple-modules-are-classified-by-dominant-highest-weights]])
by letting $\mathfrak u_J$ act by zero. Define the **generalized Verma module**

$$M_{\mathfrak p}(\lambda):=U(\mathfrak g)\otimes_{U(\mathfrak p)}E(\lambda).$$

**(3) The parabolic category.** The **parabolic category** $\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}$
is the full subcategory of $\mathcal O$ whose objects are the finitely
generated $\mathfrak h$-semisimple $\mathfrak g$-modules on which
$U(\mathfrak p)$ acts locally finitely, that is, on which every vector lies
in a finite-dimensional $\mathfrak p$-submodule; equivalently, every vector
lies in a finite-dimensional
$\mathfrak l_J$-submodule and is annihilated by a power of $\mathfrak u_J$
(local finiteness for the nilpotent $\mathfrak u_J$).

The following structural facts are part of the definition; the arguments are
given in the Remarks.

**(4) Generalized Vermas lie in $\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}$.** For each
$\mathfrak p$-dominant integral $\lambda$, $M_{\mathfrak p}(\lambda)$ is an
object of $\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}$ with highest weight $\lambda$, and the
natural surjection $M(\lambda)\twoheadrightarrow M_{\mathfrak p}(\lambda)$
exhibits $M_{\mathfrak p}(\lambda)$ as the largest quotient of the Verma
module $M(\lambda)$ that lies in $\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}$.

**(5) Simples.** The simple objects of $\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}$ are exactly
the simple highest-weight modules $L(\lambda)$ with $\lambda$
$\mathfrak p$-dominant integral
([[thm-simple-objects-of-category-o-are-highest-weight-modules]]).

**(6) Serre property.** $\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}$ is closed under subobjects,
quotients and extensions in $\mathcal O$; in particular it is an abelian
subcategory of $\mathcal O$ stable under finite direct sums.

**(7) Costandard objects.** For $\mathfrak p$-dominant integral $\lambda$ put
$\nabla_{\mathfrak p}(\lambda):=D M_{\mathfrak p}(\lambda)$, the restricted
dual of [[prop-restricted-duality-is-an-exact-involution-on-category-o]].
These are the **costandard objects** of $\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}$; each is
naturally a submodule of the ordinary dual Verma $D M(\lambda)$. They need not
be quotients of ordinary dual Vermas.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), inherited from the
published root-space and $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ suppliers. Let $\mathfrak g$ be a
finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra with Cartan subalgebra
$\mathfrak h$, root system $\Phi$
([[thm-the-root-set-is-a-reduced-crystallographic-root-system]],
[[thm-root-space-decomposition-of-a-complex-semisimple-lie-algebra]],
[[thm-root-spaces-of-a-complex-semisimple-lie-algebra-are-one-dimensional]]),
positive system $\Phi^+$ with base of simple roots
$\Delta=\{\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_r\}$
([[def-positive-system-and-base-of-simple-roots]],
[[def-reduced-crystallographic-euclidean-root-system]]), and let $J$ be a
subset of the simple indices $\{1,\dots,r\}$. Write $\Phi_J$ for the root
subsystem spanned by the simple roots indexed by $J$,
$$\Phi_J=\Phi\cap\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\{\alpha_j:j\in J\},$$
and let $H_j=h_{\alpha_j}\in\mathfrak h$ be the coroot of $\alpha_j$
([[def-coroot-of-a-lie-algebra-root]] via
[[def-killing-dual-vector-of-a-root]]). Put
$$\mathfrak h_J=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb C}\{H_j:j\in J\},\qquad \mathfrak z_J=\{h\in\mathfrak h:\alpha_j(h)=0\text{ for all }j\in J\},$$
and define the following subspaces of $\mathfrak g$, where $\mathfrak g_\alpha$
is the root space of $\alpha$
([[thm-root-space-decomposition-of-a-complex-semisimple-lie-algebra]]):

$$\mathfrak s_J=\mathfrak h_J\oplus\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\Phi_J}\mathfrak g_\alpha,\qquad \mathfrak l_J=\mathfrak s_J\oplus\mathfrak z_J=\mathfrak h\oplus\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\Phi_J}\mathfrak g_\alpha,$$
$$\mathfrak u_J=\bigoplus_{\beta\in\Phi^+\smallsetminus\Phi_J^+}\mathfrak g_\beta,\qquad \mathfrak v_J=\bigoplus_{\beta\in\Phi^-\smallsetminus\Phi_J^-}\mathfrak g_\beta,\qquad \mathfrak p_J=\mathfrak l_J\oplus\mathfrak u_J .$$

Here $\Phi_J^\pm=\Phi_J\cap\Phi^\pm$ and $\Phi^\pm$ are the positive and
negative roots with $\mathfrak n^\pm$, $\mathfrak b$ as in
[[def-positive-and-negative-nilpotent-subalgebras-and-borel-subalgebra]]. The
construction depends only on the positive system and on $J$. The following
structural facts are part of the definition (proofs and references in the
Remarks; $\operatorname{rad}$ and $\operatorname{nilrad}$ are those of
[[def-radical-of-a-finite-dimensional-lie-algebra]] and
[[def-nilradical-of-a-finite-dimensional-lie-algebra]]).

**(1) Decomposition of the Cartan.** $\mathfrak h=\mathfrak h_J\oplus\mathfrak z_J$
and $\dim\mathfrak h_J=|J|$, so $\dim\mathfrak z_J=r-|J|$.

**(2) The semisimple part.** $\mathfrak s_J$ is a Lie subalgebra of
$\mathfrak g$; it is semisimple, and its root system with respect to the
Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h_J$ is $\Phi_J$, with positive system
$\Phi_J^+$ and Weyl group $W_J=\langle s_j:j\in J\rangle\le W$
([[def-weyl-group-of-a-root-system]],
[[def-cg-parabolic-quotient-and-two-sided-minima]]).

**(3) The reductive Levi algebra.** $\mathfrak l_J$ is a Lie subalgebra with
root system $\Phi_J$ relative to $\mathfrak h$; it is reductive as in
[[def-simple-semisimple-and-reductive-lie-algebras]], with center
$\mathfrak z_J$ and derived algebra $[\mathfrak l_J,\mathfrak l_J]=\mathfrak s_J$;
$\mathfrak h$ is a Cartan subalgebra of $\mathfrak l_J$ and the Weyl group of
$(\mathfrak l_J,\mathfrak h)$ is $W_J$. The algebra $\mathfrak l_J$ need not
be semisimple: its center $\mathfrak z_J$ is nonzero as soon as $J\ne\{1,\dots,r\}$.

**(4) Parabolic and radicals.** $\mathfrak l_J$, $\mathfrak u_J$, $\mathfrak v_J$
and $\mathfrak p_J$ are Lie subalgebras
([[prop-brackets-of-root-spaces]]); $\mathfrak u_J$ is an ideal of
$\mathfrak p_J$, $\mathfrak l_J$ stabilizes $\mathfrak u_J$ and $\mathfrak v_J$,
and $\mathfrak p_J=\mathfrak l_J\ltimes\mathfrak u_J$ is a semidirect product
([[def-levi-subalgebra-and-levi-decomposition]]). Moreover
$\operatorname{nilrad}(\mathfrak p_J)=\mathfrak u_J$ and
$$\operatorname{rad}(\mathfrak p_J)=\mathfrak z_J\oplus\mathfrak u_J .$$
Consequently $[\mathfrak p_J,\mathfrak p_J]=\mathfrak s_J\oplus\mathfrak u_J$
and the quotient $\mathfrak p_J/\operatorname{rad}(\mathfrak p_J)\cong\mathfrak s_J$
is semisimple: in the sense of
[[def-levi-subalgebra-and-levi-decomposition]], $\mathfrak s_J$ is a semisimple
Levi factor of $\mathfrak p_J$ and $\mathfrak l_J$ is the reductive complement
to the nilradical. The parabolic $\mathfrak p_J$ contains $\mathfrak b$ and
$\mathfrak p_J=\mathfrak b\oplus\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\Phi_J^-}\mathfrak g_\alpha$,
the span of the negative root spaces of $\Phi_J$; for $J=\varnothing$ one has
$\mathfrak p_J=\mathfrak b$, and for $J=\{1,\dots,r\}$ one has
$\mathfrak l_J=\mathfrak s_J=\mathfrak g$ and
$\mathfrak u_J=\mathfrak v_J=0$.

**(5) The positive grading.** There exists $\zeta\in\mathfrak z_J$ with
$\alpha_j(\zeta)=0$ for $j\in J$ and $\alpha_i(\zeta)=1$ for $i\notin J$. With
respect to $\operatorname{ad}(\zeta)$ every root space $\mathfrak g_\beta$ has
weight $\beta(\zeta)$, so:

* $\mathfrak l_J$ has degree $0$ (all of $\Phi_J$ vanishes on $\zeta$);
* $\mathfrak u_J$ has strictly positive integral degrees
  $\beta(\zeta)\in\mathbb Z_{>0}$;
* $\mathfrak v_J$ has strictly negative integral degrees.

In particular $\mathfrak u_J$ is nilpotent by this positive grading, and both
$\mathfrak u_J$ and $\mathfrak v_J$ have finite-dimensional fixed-degree
slices of their PBW algebras:
$\dim U(\mathfrak u_J)_d<\infty$ and $\dim U(\mathfrak v_J)_d<\infty$ for
every $d\in\mathbb Z$ ([[thm-pbw-ordered-monomial-basis-for-the-enveloping-algebra]]).

Fix a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$, a Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$, and a positive Borel $\mathfrak b=\mathfrak h\oplus\mathfrak n^+$. Let $\{\alpha_i\}_{i\in I}$ be the simple roots of the chosen positive system and write $Q^+=\sum_{i\in I}\mathbb Z_{\geq0}\alpha_i$ and $\mu\leq\lambda$ when $\lambda-\mu\in Q^+$. Let $W$ be the Weyl group of [[def-root-reflections-and-the-weyl-group-action]] and let $\rho$ be the Weyl vector of [[def-weyl-vector-rho-for-a-chosen-positive-system]]; for $w\in W$ set $w\cdot\lambda=w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho$.

The **BGG category $\mathcal O$** is the full subcategory of left $U(\mathfrak g)$-modules $M$ satisfying all three conditions: $M$ is finitely generated; $M=\bigoplus_{\mu\in\mathfrak h^*}M_\mu$ where $M_\mu=\{v:hv=\mu(h)v\text{ for all }h\in\mathfrak h\}$; and $U(\mathfrak n^+)v$ is finite dimensional for each $v\in M$. Its morphisms are all $\mathfrak g$-linear maps. The zero module is included, generated by the empty set. The enveloping and triangular conventions are those of [[thm-pbw-ordered-monomial-basis-for-the-enveloping-algebra]] and [[thm-triangular-decomposition-from-a-chosen-positive-root-system]].

For $\lambda\in\mathfrak h^*$, the **Verma module** is the induced
$\mathfrak g$-module

$$M(\lambda):=U(\mathfrak g)\otimes_{U(\mathfrak b)}\mathbb C_\lambda,$$

where $U(\mathfrak g)$ is the quotient algebra of
[[def-universal-enveloping-algebra-as-a-tensor-quotient]] and
$\mathbb C_\lambda$ is [[def-one-dimensional-borel-module-of-weight-lambda]].
Write $v_\lambda:=1\otimes c_\lambda$.  Thus $M(\lambda)$ is the quotient of
$U(\mathfrak g)$ by the left ideal generated by $x$ for $x\in\mathfrak n^+$
and $h-\lambda(h)$ for $h\in\mathfrak h$; in particular,
$\mathfrak n^+v_\lambda=0$ and $hv_\lambda=\lambda(h)v_\lambda$.

Fix a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$, a Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$, and a positive Borel $\mathfrak b=\mathfrak h\oplus\mathfrak n^+$. Write $Q^+=\sum_i\mathbb Z_{\geq0}\alpha_i$, $\mu\leq\lambda$ when $\lambda-\mu\in Q^+$, and $w\cdot\lambda=w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho$.

The category $\mathcal O$ is closed under submodules, quotients and finite direct sums and is an abelian category. If $0\to A\to E\to B\to0$ is exact, $A,B\in\mathcal O$, and $E$ is $\mathfrak h$-semisimple, then $E\in\mathcal O$. The middle-term weight hypothesis is essential.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Every simple object
$L(\mu)$ of $\mathcal O$ admits a projective cover
$P(\mu)\twoheadrightarrow L(\mu)$
([[def-essential-epimorphism-and-projective-cover]]), which may be chosen
inside the linkage class of $\mu$; the cover is unique up to isomorphism and
indecomposable. Consequently $\mathcal O$ has enough projectives: every object
of $\mathcal O$ is a quotient of a finite direct sum of such projective
covers, because objects of $\mathcal O$ have finite length and each composition
factor is a quotient of its projective cover.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). If a projective object
$P$ of $\mathcal O$ admits an epimorphism $P\twoheadrightarrow L$ onto a
simple object $L$, then some indecomposable direct summand of $P$ maps onto
$L$, and that summand is a projective cover of $L$ (an essential epimorphism
with projective source, [[def-essential-epimorphism-and-projective-cover]]).
Any two projective covers of $L$ are isomorphic, although not canonically so,
and the endomorphism ring of a projective cover is local. In particular, for
every simple $L$ there is at most one isomorphism class of indecomposable
projectives with head $L$; when such a cover exists it is written $P(L)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice.

Fix a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$, a Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$, and a positive Borel $\mathfrak b=\mathfrak h\oplus\mathfrak n^+$. Write $Q^+=\sum_i\mathbb Z_{\geq0}\alpha_i$, $\mu\leq\lambda$ when $\lambda-\mu\in Q^+$, and $w\cdot\lambda=w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho$.

Every object of $\mathcal O$ has a finite composition series and is both Noetherian and Artinian. The length of zero is zero.

Let $\mathcal A$ be an abelian category in which every object has finite
length, and define an object to be **indecomposable** when it is nonzero and
every decomposition $X\cong Y\oplus Z$ has $Y=0$ or $Z=0$. Then:

1. every object of $\mathcal A$ is a finite direct sum of indecomposable
   objects;
2. the endomorphism ring of an indecomposable object is local, and for an
   endomorphism $f$ of an indecomposable object either $f$ is an isomorphism
   or $f$ is nilpotent;
3. the decomposition is unique up to isomorphism and permutation of the
   summands;
4. an indecomposable projective object $P$ of $\mathcal A$ has a unique
   maximal proper subobject $J(P)$, its quotient $P/J(P)$ is simple, and $P$
   is a projective cover of $P/J(P)$
   ([[def-projective-object]], [[def-essential-epimorphism-and-projective-cover]];
   projectivity here is relative to $\mathcal A$. In a full subcategory closed
   under submodules, essentiality is the superfluous-kernel condition of the
   cited module definition; projectivity in the ambient module category is
   not asserted).

Fix a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$, a Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$, and a positive Borel $\mathfrak b=\mathfrak h\oplus\mathfrak n^+$. Write $Q^+=\sum_i\mathbb Z_{\geq0}\alpha_i$, $\mu\leq\lambda$ when $\lambda-\mu\in Q^+$, and $w\cdot\lambda=w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho$.

The simple objects of $\mathcal O$ are exactly the modules $L(\lambda)$, $\lambda\in\mathfrak h^*$, and $L(\lambda)\cong L(\mu)$ if and only if $\lambda=\mu$. Simplicity here excludes zero.

Fix a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$, a Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$, and a positive Borel $\mathfrak b=\mathfrak h\oplus\mathfrak n^+$. Write $Q^+=\sum_i\mathbb Z_{\geq0}\alpha_i$, $\mu\leq\lambda$ when $\lambda-\mu\in Q^+$, and $w\cdot\lambda=w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho$.

The weights of $M(\lambda)$ are exactly $\lambda-\beta$ for

Every finite-dimensional representation of a finite-dimensional semisimple
Lie algebra over any characteristic-zero field is completely reducible.

Every finite-dimensional simple $\mathfrak g$-module is a cyclic highest-weight module whose highest weight is dominant integral, and for each dominant integral weight

$$\lambda=\sum_{i=1}^r m_i\omega_i \qquad (m_i\in \mathbb N_0),$$

there exists, up to isomorphism, a unique finite-dimensional simple module $L(\lambda)$ with highest weight $\lambda$.

Let $x_1,\dots,x_r$ be an ordered basis of a finite-dimensional complex Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$. Then the monomials

$$x_1^{a_1}x_2^{a_2}\cdots x_r^{a_r} \qquad (a_i\in \mathbb N_0)$$

form a basis of $U(\mathfrak g)$. In particular, multiplication identifies $\operatorname{gr}U(\mathfrak g)$ with the symmetric algebra $S(\mathfrak g)$ on the symbols of the $x_i$.

Fix a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$, a Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$, and a positive Borel $\mathfrak b=\mathfrak h\oplus\mathfrak n^+$. Write $Q^+=\sum_i\mathbb Z_{\geq0}\alpha_i$, $\mu\leq\lambda$ when $\lambda-\mu\in Q^+$, and $w\cdot\lambda=w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho$.

The category is the categorical direct sum $\mathcal O=\bigoplus_\chi\mathcal O_\chi$: objects have finite support in the index $\chi$, morphisms between distinct components vanish, and the canonical component projections are exact.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra with Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$, a chosen positive-root system and corresponding Borel, Weyl group $W$, and half-sum $\rho$ of positive roots. Let $\chi_\lambda$ and $\chi_\mu$ be the central characters obtained from highest weights $\lambda,\mu\in\mathfrak h^*$ for this Borel. Then

$$\chi_\lambda=\chi_\mu \quad \text{if and only if} \quad \mu\in W\cdot \lambda,$$

where $W\cdot \lambda:=\{w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho : w\in W\}$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\zeta\in\mathfrak h^*$ be a **dominant integral weight**, that is,
$\langle\zeta,\alpha_i^\vee\rangle\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$ for every simple root
$\alpha_i$ (equivalently, when $\zeta$ lies in the real span of the roots,
$\langle\zeta,\alpha^\vee\rangle\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$ for every positive root
$\alpha$). Then
$$\zeta-w\zeta\in Q^+\qquad\text{for every }w\in W,$$
where $W$ is the Weyl group of
[[def-root-reflections-and-the-weyl-group-action]] and $Q^+$ is the cone of
[[def-partial-order-on-weights]]. In particular $\zeta$ is the maximum of its
Weyl orbit for the order $\mu\le\nu$ defined by $\nu-\mu\in Q^+$, and if
$w\zeta\ge\zeta$ then $w\zeta=\zeta$.

Consequently, if $\lambda$ is a weight with $\lambda+\rho$ dominant integral
($\rho$ the Weyl vector of [[def-weyl-vector-rho-for-a-chosen-positive-system]]),
then $\lambda-w\mathbin\cdot\lambda\in Q^+$ for every $w\in W$, and $\lambda$
is the maximum of its linkage class $W_\lambda\mathbin\cdot\lambda$ of
[[def-integral-weyl-group-of-a-weight]]; here
$W_\lambda=W$ because every simple reflection pairs integrally with
$\lambda+\rho$.

Integrality is used with its full strength: for a dominant $\zeta$ that is not
integral the conclusion $\zeta-w\zeta\in Q^+$ fails for reflections pairing
non-integrally with $\zeta$, and only the reflections integral at $\zeta$ can
be used.

Assume the Axiom of Choice.

Fix a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$, a Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$, and a positive Borel $\mathfrak b=\mathfrak h\oplus\mathfrak n^+$. Write $Q^+=\sum_i\mathbb Z_{\geq0}\alpha_i$, $\mu\leq\lambda$ when $\lambda-\mu\in Q^+$, and $w\cdot\lambda=w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho$.

Restricted Chevalley duality is an exact contravariant equivalence $D:\mathcal O\to\mathcal O^{\mathrm{op}}$, with a natural isomorphism $D^2\cong\operatorname{id}$. It preserves each weight-space dimension, the formal character, and every simple composition multiplicity.

An object $P$ of an abelian category is **projective** when for every epimorphism
$q:E\twoheadrightarrow M$ and every morphism $f:P\to M$, there exists a
morphism $\widetilde f:P\to E$ with

$$q\widetilde f=f.$$

The lift $\widetilde f$ need not be unique.

An object $I$ of an abelian category is **injective** when for every monomorphism
$m:M\rightarrowtail E$ and every morphism $f:M\to I$, there exists a morphism
$\widetilde f:E\to I$ with

$$\widetilde f\,m=f.$$

The extension $\widetilde f$ need not be unique.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: **Simples and standards.** By [F1], Levi-dominant integral highest weights are exactly the simple labels in $\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}$. Their generalized standards are quotients of the ordinary Vermas with the same one-dimensional highest-weight space and simple head. They have finite length by [F2], and their weights, and hence highest weights of composition factors, lie in $\lambda-Q^+$ by [F3]. For any parabolic quotient of the ordinary Verma, the image of its highest vector is killed by the full positive nilpotent algebra. Its finite Levi span is the cyclic highest-weight simple $E(\lambda)$ by complete reducibility, and the radical kills that span since it kills the highest vector and is Levi-stable. The induction universal property therefore factors the quotient map through $\Delta_{\mathfrak p}(\lambda)$. This proves the largest-quotient assertion locally. This proves parts (1) and (2).

**Largest locally finite quotient.** For $M\in\mathcal O$, let $\mathcal K$ be the set of its subobjects $K$ such that $M/K\in\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}$. It contains $M$, and finite length bounds $\ell(M/K)$, so choose $K_0$ for which this quotient length is maximal. For every $K\in\mathcal K$, the diagonal map embeds $M/(K\cap K_0)$ in $M/K\oplus M/K_0$. Serre closure gives $K\cap K_0\in\mathcal K$. Maximality and the epimorphism $M/(K\cap K_0)\to M/K_0$ force equality of lengths; its kernel is therefore zero and $K_0\subseteq K$. Thus $K_0$ is the least kernel among all parabolic quotients. For a map $M\to V$ with $V$ parabolic, its image is parabolic and its kernel lies in $\mathcal K$, so the map factors uniquely through $M/K_0$. This proves the functorial universal property of $L_{\mathfrak p}M=M/K_0$ and its left adjunction to the exact inclusion. It is right exact as a left adjoint.

**The correct Hom arrows.** The ordinary Verma surjection is $M(\eta)\twoheadrightarrow\Delta_{\mathfrak p}(\eta)$, and the costandard inclusion is $\nabla_{\mathfrak p}(\xi)\hookrightarrow DM(\xi)$. Composing with these maps injects parabolic $\operatorname{Hom}(\Delta_{\mathfrak p}(\eta),\nabla_{\mathfrak p}(\xi))$ into the ordinary standard-costandard Hom of [F3]. Thus it is zero for different labels and at most one-dimensional for equal labels. In the equal case the nonzero composite through $L(\eta)$ is a homomorphism from the standard head to the costandard socle, so its dimension is one.

**Every parabolic standard-costandard extension splits.** Consider $0	o
abla_{\mathfrak p}(\xi)	o X	o\Delta_{\mathfrak p}(\eta)	o0$. First suppose $\xi-\eta
otin Q^+\setminus\{0\}$, including equality and incomparability. Choose a weight-$\eta$ lift $v$ of the source highest vector. If a positive root vector sent $v$ nontrivially to weight $\eta+\alpha$, its image in the standard quotient would be zero, so this weight would occur in the costandard. But all costandard weights are $\le\xi$; hence $\eta<\eta+\alpha\le\xi$ would imply $\eta<\xi$, contrary to the case assumption. Thus $v$ is killed by every positive root vector. Its Levi span is finite dimensional because $X$ is locally parabolic-finite. By [F4] it is the cyclic finite Levi highest-weight simple $E(\eta)$: complete reducibility decomposes the span, and the nonzero components of a highest-weight vector of weight $\eta$ belong to copies of that same simple, with cyclic diagonal span one copy. The radical kills this whole span since it kills $v$ and $[\mathfrak l,\mathfrak u]\subseteq\mathfrak u$. Induction therefore gives a map $\Delta_{\mathfrak p}(\eta)	o X$ whose composite onto the quotient is the identity on its generating top, hence the identity. The extension splits. In the remaining case $\eta<\xi$, duality gives an extension with reversed pair $(\xi,\eta)$, to which the first case applies; dualizing the splitting back finishes the proof. Consequently parabolic $\operatorname{Ext}^1(\Delta_{\mathfrak p}(\eta),
abla_{\mathfrak p}(\xi))=0$ for every pair, proved inside this category. The argument uses the absence of a weight obtained by raising the chosen top, not a total ordering of incomparable highest weights.

**Finite bounded projectives in an integral summand.** Fix such a central-character summand $\chi$, with dot-dominant $\kappa$ from [F5]. Every weight of every object in it is $\le\kappa$, because its composition factors have highest labels in that dot orbit. The grading element has nonnegative value on $Q^+$, so every $\zeta$-weight is at most $\kappa(\zeta)$. For a parabolic label $\eta$ put $d=\kappa(\zeta)-\eta(\zeta)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$ and let $E=E(\eta)$. Define the finite-dimensional $\mathfrak p$-module $B_{\le d}(E)$ by inducing $E$ from the Levi to $\mathfrak p$ and quotienting by all positive-radical PBW terms of $\zeta$-degree greater than $d$. These terms form a submodule since the Levi preserves degree and the radical increases it. On every object $W$ in the summand, a Levi map $E\to W$ automatically kills the excluded terms after extension to $U(\mathfrak p)\otimes_{U(\mathfrak l)}E$, as their weights exceed the bound. The descending radical-degree filtration of this finite module has semisimple Levi slices killed by the radical; exact PBW induction gives a finite generalized-standard flag and places its induction in $\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}$ before central projection. Thus $Q(E)=\operatorname{pr}_\chi(U(\mathfrak g)\otimes_B B_{\le d}(E))$ represents $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak l}(E,W)$. This functor is exact: lift a basis of any finite Levi image through an epimorphism, take the finite sum of the Levi spans of those lifts, and split the resulting finite Levi epimorphism by [F4]. Hence $Q(E)$ is projective in this summand and maps onto $L(\eta)$.

**Projective covers and enough projectives.** The adjunction gives $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O^{\mathfrak p}}(L_{\mathfrak p}P,-)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O}(P,-)$ on the parabolic subcategory, so an ordinary projective has parabolic projective image. For a parabolic simple $L(\lambda)$, apply $L_{\mathfrak p}$ to the ordinary projective cover to obtain $L_{\mathfrak p}P^{(\mathcal O)}(\lambda)\twoheadrightarrow L(\lambda)$. If a subobject of this image surjects onto the simple, its inverse image in the ordinary cover does also and is the whole cover by essentiality. Hence the image map is essential and is the required parabolic projective cover. An ordinary projective epimorphism onto any parabolic object becomes a parabolic projective epimorphism by right exactness. Dualizing gives enough injectives. This proves part (3) on all the objects in the stated parabolic category.

**These projectives begin with actual PBW flags.** Filter $B_{\le d}(E)$ by descending radical degree. Each degree slice is finite-dimensional and semisimple for the Levi, with radical acting by zero on the slice. PBW makes induction from $B$ exact, so inducing this filtration gives a finite generalized-standard flag on $U(\mathfrak g)\otimes_B B_{\le d}(E)$. A generalized standard has scalar central character, because its ordinary Verma precursor does; exact central projection therefore either retains or kills each whole standard slice. Hence $Q(E)$ has an actual finite generalized-standard flag. As an $N$-module the unprojected induction is graded free of finite rank, with basis the finite graded space $B_{\le d}(E)$. Central projection is an $N$-linear grading-preserving direct-summand projection. Every parabolic projective cover in the chosen summand is a grading-preserving summand of the corresponding $Q(E)$: lift the epimorphism $Q(E)\to L(\eta)$ to its cover, use essentiality for surjectivity, then split by projectivity.

**Graded direct summands stay free.** For a graded $N$-module bounded above, the equality $V=N_{<0}V$ forces $V=0$: a nonzero homogeneous component of highest occupied degree cannot be obtained from strictly higher-degree components. Let $R$ be a grading-preserving direct summand of a finite graded free $N$-module. Then $R/N_{<0}R$ is finite dimensional. Choose a homogeneous basis of this quotient and lifts to $R$, giving a map from a finite graded free module $G$ onto $R$; its cokernel is bounded above and equals its own $N_{<0}$ multiple, so the map is surjective by the preceding argument. It splits as a graded $N$-map since $R$ is a graded projective summand. The kernel $K$ then has $K/N_{<0}K=0$, because the induced map on generator quotients is an isomorphism and reduction of the split sequence is split exact. The same bounded-above argument gives $K=0$. Thus $R$ is graded free of finite rank. This proves the summand claim without importing the flag criterion or assuming finite-dimensional degree-zero pieces of an enveloping Levi algebra.

**Free finite rank gives generalized-standard flags.** Let $R$ be one of these parabolic $\mathfrak g$-modules, graded free of finite $N$-rank. Within its fixed $\zeta$-eigenvalue coset its degrees are bounded above and its components finite dimensional. Let $a$ be its highest occupied degree. The finite Levi module $R_a$ is semisimple and the positive radical kills it, as it raises degree. A homogeneous free basis shows that all its degree-$a$ basis vectors are part of an $N$-basis, so the induction map $U(\mathfrak g)\otimes_B R_a=N\otimes R_a\to R$ is injective and its quotient is again graded free, with those finitely many generators removed. Decomposing $R_a$ into finite Levi simples gives an actual submodule that is a finite sum of generalized standards. Repeating on the quotient terminates since each step reduces the finite $N$-rank. All subobjects and quotients lie in the selected central summand; hence their simple Levi labels are the allowed labels there. This proves that every projective cover, and therefore every finite sum and summand of them, has a finite generalized-standard flag. The grading is only the actual semisimple $\zeta$-action, shifted on its coset; it is not a Koszul assumption. This proves the flag part of (4).

**Reciprocity.** For a generalized-standard flag of $P^{\mathfrak p}(\lambda)$, steps 1.3 and 1.4 make $\operatorname{Hom}(-,
abla_{\mathfrak p}(\mu))$ exact along its flag sequences and show that its dimension counts precisely the $\Delta_{\mathfrak p}(\mu)$ sections. On the other hand projectivity makes $\operatorname{Hom}(P^{\mathfrak p}(\lambda),-)$ exact along a composition series of $
abla_{\mathfrak p}(\mu)$. Its value on a simple has dimension one for $L(\lambda)$ and zero for every other label, by the essential simple head of the projective cover. Consequently $(P^{\mathfrak p}(\lambda):\Delta_{\mathfrak p}(\mu))=[
abla_{\mathfrak p}(\mu):L(\lambda)]=[\Delta_{\mathfrak p}(\mu):L(\lambda)]$, the last equality by simple-preserving duality. This also proves independence of flag multiplicities and their finiteness. By standard support, only $\mu\ge\lambda$ occurs, and the diagonal multiplicity is one.

**Labelled standard quotient and its higher-standard kernel.** The same lifting argument as in step 1.4, with $\Delta_{\mathfrak p}(\beta)$ in place of the costandard, shows $\operatorname{Ext}^1(\Delta_{\mathfrak p}(\alpha),\Delta_{\mathfrak p}(\beta))=0$ whenever $\alpha\not<\beta$: its submodule has no weight strictly above the lifted top $\alpha$, and finite Levi splitting supplies the section. In the flag of $P^{\mathfrak p}(\lambda)$ from step 5.1, the labelled standard occurs once and every other standard has strictly higher label by step 6.1. Whenever the labelled standard precedes a higher standard in the flag, the corresponding two-section subquotient splits by this Ext vanishing. Swapping those two sections moves the labelled standard upwards in the flag; finitely many swaps place it last. Thus there is an actual epimorphism $P^{\mathfrak p}(\lambda)\to\Delta_{\mathfrak p}(\lambda)$ with a kernel having a finite flag of strictly higher standards. This is the highest-weight projective-kernel axiom, obtained without the tilting or homological-criterion suppliers.

**Bases, characters and conclusion.** In the fixed integral summand there are finitely many allowed labels by [F5]. Their simple classes form its finite-length Grothendieck basis; the standard-to-simple matrix has diagonal one and entries only below the diagonal after a linear extension of the root order. It is therefore invertible over $\mathbb Z$, so standard classes give another basis. A finite relation between the simple characters has a maximal highest-weight label with a nonzero coefficient; its highest-weight monomial occurs in that simple with coefficient one and in no remaining incomparable or lower simple, so the relation cannot vanish. Inducting proves that characters are injective on this Grothendieck group. The constructions above establish the simples and standard support, the reflector and enough projectives, the local Hom/Ext orthogonality, actual generalized-standard flags, reciprocity and the labelled higher-standard kernel. Duality has remained the ordinary restricted duality restricted to the actual parabolic subcategory. These are all four parts of the Statement.
